name: East Face
beta: From below the E side of the formation, work up a series of zig-zagging ledges to the summit; a short 4th-class perfect hand-crack section is one of the standard variations. Little to no protection is typically placed.
overview: A less-traveled line up Witches Tower's east/southeast aspect, climbing broken, blocky Class 4 terrain; only a handful of ascents are on record (it is logged as a 4th-class rock route that's occasionally graded up to Ice 2/Mixed 1b, reflecting a short snow or low-angle ice step that can persist on the upper face into early summer).

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (~3,400 ft, reached via ~8.7 mi of Icicle Creek Road southwest of Leavenworth), follow the Stuart Lake Trail south along Mountaineer Creek. At about 2.5 miles, bear left (south) at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (this junction is also where the Lake Stuart fork continues straight); the trail crosses Mountaineer Creek on a log/boulder crossing that can be a wet, awkward ford in early season high water. Continue climbing through forest and over a boulder field to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) at roughly 4.3 miles from the trailhead — this is the last reliable, easily accessed water source and most parties treat water here before pushing on. Skirt the lake's west shore and its south end on climbers' trail through talus to the base of the infamous Aasgard Pass climb: an unmaintained, badly eroded boot-path that gains roughly 2,200-2,500 ft in well under a mile of steep, loose scree, boulders and (through at least June, sometimes into July) lingering snow/ice that can require an ice axe and even crampons or micro-spikes — this is the single biggest approach hazard and crux of the day, with real rockfall risk from parties above and easy route-finding mistakes in cloud or whiteout. Top out at Aasgard Pass (~7,750-7,800 ft), roughly 5 miles and ~4,400 ft above the trailhead. From the pass, work uphill to the south and southwest across talus and boulders toward the tower, then around beneath its east-facing aspect, staying high along the rim of the Enchantment basin; expect additional short snow patches and blocky talus underfoot right up to the base of the face, with no water beyond what you carried from Colchuck Lake or scooped from snowmelt trickles.
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass, then south and southwest to the light-coloured rock below Dragontail's south ridge
current.descent: Witches Tower's E/SE Face is a short route — one pitch of fourth-class climbing up the light-colored ("white rock") face to the small, exposed summit block — so full-rope-length rappelling is not mandatory, but many parties prefer not to reverse the exposed ledges. The commonly used descent is to downclimb/scramble off the South Face or Southwest Corner side (Class 2-4, the same terrain used as the standard walk-up/scramble route) back down to the notch/col southwest of the tower, then rejoin the Aasgard Pass approach for the hike out. Where climbers do rope up for the final step off the summit or down the face itself, expect a single ~100-150 ft rappel from natural gear — a slung horn, block, or tree rather than fixed bolts; a single 60m rope doubled (30m per strand) or even a 30m rope run single-strand is enough for this one rappel. Descent-specific hazards: exposed, sometimes loose/exfoliating granite on the upper face and summit block, fast-moving afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed summit with no quick retreat, and then the long, knee-jarring downclimb of Aasgard Pass's loose talus/scree back to Colchuck Lake, which many parties find harder and slower than the ascent, especially with residual snow/ice underfoot.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack (a few small-to-medium cams and nuts) can be carried for the short 4th-class hand-crack variation, but many parties climb this route with little to no protection.
current.pro_needs: The main gear requirement is simply sturdy boots; protection is optional given the low difficulty, though the short hand-crack section can be backed up with small cams if desired.
bivy: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
current.rope_note: Published descriptions list Witches Tower's east-facing route (matching E/SE Face) as a mixed-grade line: 4th class base with 5.6/5.10a/5.10b variations higher/direct. The 4th-class line noted here corresponds to the easiest (original) line up the white rock.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From a high parking area on FR6517 about 0.5 mile east of the summit, the route gains about 1,460 ft in all, finishing with roughly 600 vertical feet of open slope/talus to the top — easy class 2 if you stay to the right side, or class 2/3 up the center. Total distance is well under a mile each way, and the round trip from the car is typically under three hours. The peak sees very few visitors compared to nearby Beckler Peak and Evergreen Mountain.
overview: Eagle Rock is a prominent, blocky summit (5,614 ft, about 1,400 ft of prominence) on the ridge between the Beckler River and Skykomish valleys near Stevens Pass. From the FR6517 trailhead (elev. ~4,150 ft), it's roughly 0.8 miles one-way and about 1,460 ft of gain to the top — a short outing (often under 3 hours round trip) for a big, airy summit panorama over the US-2 corridor peaks, the Beckler and North Fork Skykomish drainages, and (on clear days) Glacier Peak and the Monte Cristo group. The route finishes with a Class 2–3 scramble on blocky rock.

current.approach: Drive the Beckler River Road (FR-65) out of Skykomish and follow it into the FR-6510/FR-6514/FR-6517 spur network (about 10.8 miles of gravel/dirt forest road past the pavement) to road's end, roughly 0.5 mile east of Eagle Rock's summit at about 4,150 ft — this is the trailhead; there is no maintained trail beyond it. From the parking area, leave the road and head west/southwest straight up the hillside cross-country. You break out of brush and into open forest within the first few hundred feet, then continue uphill through timber; after a few hundred yards the trees give way to open talus slopes below the cliff bands on Eagle Rock's northeast side. From the base of the talus, do not push straight up into the cliffs — instead make an ascending, counterclockwise (climber's-left) traverse across and around the north side of the peak to a broad bench/step at roughly 5,000 ft. From that step, angle southwest a few hundred yards to the base of the final summit slope, where the scramble proper begins. One-way distance from the car to the summit is only about 0.8 mile, but essentially all of the route's ~1,400 ft of gain is packed into that short distance, so it feels considerably steeper than the mileage implies. There is no reliable water source anywhere on the approach — carry all the water you need from the car. Hazards are mostly footing and route-finding: loose talus and scree on the traverse, brush low down, no trail or cairns to follow, and cliff bands that will cliff out parties who try to go straight up the northeast talus instead of arcing counterclockwise. In late September 2024 the gate low on the Beckler spur network was locked, adding about ten miles of road each way; the road beyond it is rutted but passable to an AWD or high-clearance vehicle. Another party in early October found that gate closed but unlocked. Check before driving.
approach_variant_names: FR-6517 road end and the counterclockwise traverse
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line. The one place that is not a plain walk-off is the lower cliff band on the north side, roughly 15 m of slabby rock and loose dirt. In dry weather it downclimbs at class 3; wet, mossy or snowy it is closer to class 4 and most parties rope it. Walk the steep forest above it, belay off a tree just above the band, and make a single rappel of about 15 m (a 30 m rope with a sling and a rappel ring covers it). Do not rely on rope or webbing left on the slope by earlier parties. Below the band, continue the talus traverse back to treeline and the road end.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard route — it is a class 2-3 scramble on open slope/talus requiring no rope, protection, or anchors.
current.pro_needs: None; the standard line is unroped scrambling terrain throughout.
current.rope_note: Standard route: talus below cliffs on the NE side, an ascending counterclockwise traverse around the mountain (the route's crux section), then ~600 ft of Class 2 (or Class 2/3 direct) to the summit.

name: Southwest Ridge
beta: The standard route follows the Bean Creek Trail from the Beverly Turnpike Trailhead up the Bean Creek drainage to Earl Pass, then climbs the southwest ridge on intermittent tread to the summit. It is rated class 2 in dry summer conditions but is also a popular spring snow scramble that can require an ice axe and crampons on the steep, icy south-facing summit slopes.
overview: On the southeastern edge of the Stuart Range above the Beverly-Turnpike country, Earl Peak is a friendly nontechnical summit offering broad views toward Mount Stuart. The southwest ridge is an enjoyable hike-and-scramble outing popular as a conditioner and viewpoint.

current.approach: In 2026 FR-9737-112 is washed out and barricaded at the bottom, so walk its final mile-plus to the Beverly Creek Trailhead (at ~3,600 ft); from there, start on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391. After a short, mellow half mile paralleling Beverly Creek, bear right at the signed junction onto the Bean Creek Trail (#1391A), leaving the Turnpike Trail behind. The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest and then opens into Bean Creek Basin around the 2.5-mile mark — a broad, flower-choked meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats; this is the scenic highlight of the approach and a natural rest/water stop. Bean Creek itself is the last dependable water source. Its crossings are easy rock-hops by mid-to-late summer but can be swift, cold, and genuinely hazardous during May–June snowmelt, so plan accordingly if going early season. Beyond the basin the trail (tread becomes intermittent in the upper meadows) climbs switchbacks up to Earl Pass at roughly 6,200 ft — the broad saddle on the divide between the Bean Creek and Standup Creek drainages, about 3.5–4 miles and ~2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. This pass has scattered flat tent sites and is the standard high camp for parties splitting the trip, or the pack-cache point for day-scramblers. From Earl Pass, leave the trail and pick up the boot path climbing the southwest ridge directly toward the summit. This final ~800 vertical feet is the crux of the trip: a sustained, unrelenting class 2 scramble on loose scree, sand, and broken rock with only an intermittent climbers' track — go slow, test holds, and be mindful of kicking rock onto anyone below. The ridge tops out on Earl Peak's 7,036-ft summit with a full panorama of the Stuart Range from Mt. Stuart to Argonaut, Colchuck, and Dragontail.
approach_variant_names: Bean Creek Trail to Earl Pass
Standup Creek trail
current.descent: This is a walk-off — no rappelling is involved. Descend by reversing the ascent line: pick your way back down the loose, steep southwest ridge scree/sand to Earl Pass, using extra caution on the descent since loose rock and sandy scree are more prone to sliding underfoot going downhill, and stick to the established boot path where possible to limit erosion and rockfall onto other parties. From Earl Pass, rejoin and follow the Bean Creek Trail back down through Bean Creek Basin (re-crossing Bean Creek — again a hazard consideration in early-season high water) and the short connector back onto the Beverly Turnpike Trail to the Beverly Creek Trailhead. In poor visibility, the upper boot path across the open ridge can be hard to follow, so note landmarks (or track your ascent) on the way up. Some parties extend the day with an easy ridge traverse over to neighboring Bean Peak before dropping back to Earl Pass, but the standard descent is the straightforward reverse of the SW ridge/Bean Creek approach.
current.detailed_rack: No technical gear required.
current.pro_needs: None.
bivy: Teanaway Community Forest campgrounds — 29 Pines, Teanaway Campground and Indian Camp

name: Standup Creek Route
beta: From a trailhead off Standup Creek Road, follow the Standup Creek Trail (#1369) up an old roadbed, crossing Standup Creek six to seven times (the first crossing is the largest; later ones range from brushy to easy rock-hops), passing wildflower meadows and a small waterfall, then switchbacking through forest to reach a ~6,200-ft saddle shared with the Bean Creek Trail approach — about 3,200 ft of gain over roughly 4.5 miles. From there the route joins the same open ridge crest used by the Southwest Ridge for the final ~0.7 mile / 900 ft scramble to the summit, described by longtime climbers as non-technical except a short step onto the summit block.
overview: A quieter, less-traveled alternate approach to Earl Peak's summit from the east via the Standup Creek Trail, which gains a ridge/saddle joining the same upper scramble used by the Southwest Ridge route.

current.approach: Access is via Standup Creek Road, reached from Stafford Creek Road off the Teanaway River Road near Cle Elum. The Standup Creek Trail #1369 follows an old road with little early elevation gain, crosses Standup Creek six to seven times, passes through brushy sections with some downed trees, then switchbacks up through forest and meadows to the ~6,200-ft saddle at the head of the drainage. The Labor Mountain Fire closure order on this trail has been lifted, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026; expect burned forest and downed trees in the drainage.
current.descent: Reverse the ridge scramble back to the ~6,200-ft saddle, then descend the Standup Creek Trail back through its creek crossings to the trailhead, or continue over the saddle onto the Bean Creek Trail to exit via Beverly Creek Trailhead if running a loop/shuttle.
current.detailed_rack: No rack used; treated as an unroped scramble.

name: East Face
beta: Traverse right from start toward the large hanging 'split block'. Pitch 1 offers a 5.8 finger crack or easier ground to its right, and pitch 2 has a critical 25-30 foot unprotectable section on a dyke. Pitch 3 climbs through a chimney and dirty corner. The final pitch offers laid-back climbing in an obvious corner approach to summit, though the final moves to the horned summit are unprotectable. Light rack to 3 inches adequate. The route requires careful rock quality assessment and awareness of unprotected sections.
overview: A 4-pitch alpine climb on high-quality granite featuring moderate climbing with runout sections and an unprotectable summit block. The East Face is rarely climbed but provides direct access to the distinctive horned summit. This is a worthwhile alpine rock objective for parties comfortable with runout climbing and willing to accept the inherent risks.

current.approach: Access via SR-20 north of Cascade Loop; drive past the hairpin turn just east of Washington Pass to the pullout near Milepost 166 on the south side of the highway. A climbers trail drops from the pullout, immediately crosses Early Winters Creek, and ascends steeply through timbered terrain to a bench camp around 6,500 feet. From camp, continue east toward the Wine Spires. From the bench camp, traverse to approach Chablis Spire via Burgundy Col approach (recommended spring-fall; 2-5 hours total from trailhead) or via Silver Star Creek drainage (recommended for winter; approach in snow). Chablis is reached after traversing past or over Burgundy Col area.
approach_variant_names: Burgundy Col, then down and south under the east faces
current.descent: From the summit area, downclimb via loose blocks and corners to locate the large granite horn with established sling anchor. This is a critical waypoint. Thread both 60m ropes through the horn slings. First double-rope rappel descends to the large slung horn at the top of pitch 2. Reanchor ropes there for the second rappel to complete descent to scree base of East Face. Exercise caution for rockfall and loose rock throughout the descent process.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack to 3 inches: 1-2 sets of quickdraws for potential fixed anchors, single set of traditional cams (0.5-3"), supplemented with small wired nuts (RZA or similar), 4-6 slings of various lengths, two 60m dynamic ropes (single strand rated), locking carabiners.
rack: Light cam rack 0.5–3in + small wired nuts
current.pro_needs: Light traditional rock rack through 3 inches. Natural protection abundant from granite flakes and crack systems, but Pitch 2 includes a 25-30 foot dyke section with limited pro. Two 60m ropes required for two-rappel descent. Sling and carabiner anchor kit essential. No ice tools required on standard East Face route.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
current.rope_note: 4-pitch route on Chablis Spire (Wine Spires, Washington Pass), every pitch is about 5.6, and the short unprotected dyke on P2 is the one serious section. Descent: downclimb 15ft from the 'bunny ears' notch to rap slings on a horn, then two double-rope rappels to the base, the second from the slung horn at the top of pitch 2.

name: East Face
beta: From high camp, ascend moraine to the Chimney Glacier, cross the bergschrund via snow/ice blocks, then scramble exposed 4th-class ledges to the Main Notch between the South and Main peaks. From the notch, a 3rd/4th-class 'reddish ramp' and further scrambling lead to a broad ledge below the summit tower, where climbers rack up for 3 roped pitches to the top. Rock is generally sound but has loose ('choss') sections; many parties note the bergschrund/moat crossing is often the technical crux of the day, not the rock pitches.
overview: The East Face is Chimney Rock's most commonly climbed and documented line to the true Main/Central Summit (7,727 ft) — the same summit reached by the peak's 1930 first ascent. From a high camp near the toe of the Chimney Glacier, parties rope up and cross the glacier and its bergschrund/moat to reach three pitches of low-fifth-class (5.3) rock: a lichen-covered chimney, an exposed 4th-class traverse, and a final chimney that tops out just below the summit cairn. It's a long, remote objective — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip, with roughly 19 miles and 6,000 ft of elevation gain/loss round trip from the Pete Lake Trailhead.

current.approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake about a mile, through Lemah Meadow, to the Pacific Crest Trail junction and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber at an obvious logjam that serves as the creek crossing, and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. A rock buttress called Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft), overlooking Chimney Creek's waterfalls, marks the top of the brush; most parties reach it in 4-5 hours from the trailhead. Sunrise Knob and flat-topped boulder sites with water in the basins at about 4,600-4,800 ft are the usual high camps (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip); from camp the moraine leads up to the toe of the Chimney Glacier. Reliable water is at Pete Lake and the low Chimney Creek crossings; above the moraine plan on melting snow or glacier water. Hazards: the avalanche-path crossing (blowdown, lingering snow/avalanche debris into early summer), loose/brushy ravine crossings, and standard glacier travel hazards (crevasses, moats) gaining and crossing the Chimney Glacier to the base of the route.
approach_variant_names: Pete Lake trail and the PCT, then the Chimney Creek climbers' path to the moraine basin
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two rappels on a single rope; some parties make three), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
current.detailed_rack: Light-to-moderate alpine trad rack: stoppers/nuts, cams up to ~3 inches, plenty of slings, and spare webbing/cord for weathered rappel anchors.
current.pro_needs: A moderate trad rack (stoppers plus cams roughly 0.5–1 inch) covers the crux chimney and ledge systems; bring extra slings for tat at rappel anchors.
bivy: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
current.rope_note: Standard East Face route: P1 vegetated chimney, P2 exposed slab to a ledge, P3 deep summit chimney — low 5th class throughout, consistent with the 5.3 grade given (distinct from the harder 5.6 'East Face Direct' variant).

name: Northeast Buttress ("Come Over to the Dark Side")
beta: Established over 3 days in September 2008 by Alan Kearney and Erik Johnson (a route Kearney had attempted in 1991 and 2003), the line follows the peak's northeast buttress up compact gneiss with few natural crack systems. The pair placed small cams and numerous knifeblade and bugaboo pitons for protection and drilled no bolts; the route is described as featuring dark, brooding overhangs, a delicate traverse, sections of blank rock, and loose, teetering blocks near the top.
overview: A long, sustained new-wave buttress route up East McMillan Spire's dramatic 2,400-foot northeast wall, climbing compact Skagit gneiss on mostly moderate (5.6-5.8) rock with a handful of 5.9 pitches and three or four pitches of 5.10-.

current.approach: A roughly two-day approach traveling via the remnants of the McMillan Creek glaciers to reach the base of the peak's north side/northeast buttress; on the day of the climb the party hiked about 3.5 hours from a high camp to the base of the wall.
current.descent: The first-ascent party descended by rappelling back down through the upper north face and the north/northeast buttress system over the course of a day, retracing the general line of ascent to their camp below the wall.
current.detailed_rack: A standard free rack of small-to-medium cams and stoppers, plus a selection of knifeblade and bugaboo pitons for the compact, discontinuous-crack sections; no bolts were placed on the first ascent, so parties should be prepared to place or find natural gear on runout terrain.
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin and insecure on much of the compact gneiss; carry pitons (knifeblades/bugaboos) in addition to a small-cam rack, and expect some runout, low-protection pitches, particularly on the crux 5.10- sections.

name: East Ridge
beta: Roughly three-quarters of parties climb Snowking via this East/Kindy Ridge line, the least technically demanding of the mountain's four recognized routes (the others being the Northwest Route, West Route, and Illabot Creek Route). From an overnight camp near Cyclone Lake or higher on the ridge, follow heather benches and easy slabs up the ridge crest, staying near the crest and side-hilling around minor gendarmes and cliff bands where the ridge is blocked — the route's technical crux, rated around Class 3. The final few hundred feet climb easy snow/scree below the summit block, staying off the Snowking Glacier proper, before a Class 3 scramble tops out from the south/SSE side.
overview: The East Ridge is Snowking Mountain's fastest, least-technical, non-glaciated line to the summit. It shares the same brushy FR-1570/Kindy Ridge approach and Cyclone Lake camp as the standard glacier route, then climbs heather benches and easy slabs up the ridge on the mountain's east side rather than crossing the Snowking Glacier. From the meadows east of Cyclone Lake it's roughly a two-hour, 2,000-foot Class 2-3 scramble to the 7,433-7,439 ft summit, with good bivy sites and snowmelt water at about 6,300 ft and 6,900 ft directly on the ridge for parties who want to split the summit day. Because it stays off the glacier, it's a popular late-season option once the Snowking Glacier opens up with exposed crevasses.

current.approach: From Marblemount, drive Cascade River Road ~14.2 miles to the signed FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road) junction and turn right. Cross the Cascade River on a concrete bridge and continue ~0.4 mile to a Y junction where the right fork is blocked by boulders — park here (roughly 1,150-1,300 ft; a long-standing washout on FR-1570 keeps most parties from driving any higher). A climbers' trail flagged with pink ribbon every 50-150 ft leaves the old roadbed and climbs steeply and directly through old growth — about 1,700 vertical ft in the first mile — to a ridge saddle near Point 5116. At the saddle there is an easy-to-miss junction: go left and climb roughly 1,000 ft to Peak 5791, then traverse heather benches and meadows above Cyclone Lake, crossing or contouring Peak 5860, to reach the base of Snowking's East Ridge. Figure ~5 hours and ~5,000 ft of gain from the car to the Cyclone Lake/ridge base. In mid-June the climbers path was patchy from about 4,600 ft and the forest snow stayed firm even in the afternoon; the road needed medium clearance for stream crossings. In early July snow patches began near 5,100 ft and became continuous around the tarns by Cyclone Lake; running meltwater was available but dries once the snow is gone. The approach is a roller-coaster of small ups and downs over Found Peak and the ridge, so the day totals much more climbing than the summit height suggests, roughly 8,500-9,000 ft round trip.
approach_variant_names: The Kindy Creek roadbed and the ribbon-marked climbers' trail to the Point 5116 saddle
Camping at the lake below the ridge
current.descent: Reverse the East Ridge back to the Cyclone Lake basin, then retrace the flagged Kindy Ridge climbers' trail down to the FR-1570 parking area. In early season with good snow coverage, some parties glissade sections above Cyclone Lake; by late summer these slopes are bare talus and heather, so it's a walk-down.
current.detailed_rack: None -- an unroped Class 2-3 scramble; no rope or rack typically needed once the trail and ridge are snow-free.
current.pro_needs: None — an unroped Class 2-3 scramble; no rack or rope is typically carried.
bivy: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle

name: East Ridge
beta: From the Cedar Creek Trailhead, gain the ridge early and follow its crest essentially the whole way to the summit, passing several sub-summits along the way. Route-finding on loose rock is the main challenge; difficulty rises to 5.9+ V or harder if a party ropes up earlier or maintains continuous contact with the ridge crest.
overview: A committing, mostly-unroped 3.5-mile alpine ridge traverse from the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks to Silver Star's east summit (8,876 ft). First completed by Geof Childs and Larry Goldie on September 14, 2000 in 14 hours car-to-car, placing no protection and belaying no pitches other than two short rappels near Varden Col. Sustained exposure, loose rock, and long stretches of solo 4th/low-5th-class climbing make it a serious, rarely-repeated outing on a different trailhead/approach than the peak's standard Silver Star Glacier route.

current.approach: Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama -- a different trailhead than the Silver Star Creek/Highway 20 pullout used for the Glacier and NE Ridge routes -- and gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Cedar Creek Trailhead near Mazama, gaining the ridge at the Cedar and Early Winters Creek confluence
current.descent: From the summit, rope down or downclimb a short distance to gain the Silver Star Glacier, then descend the glacier west/northwest toward Burgundy Col. From the col, climb/hike up and over to the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops back to Highway 20 near milepost 166 (roughly 4 miles from Washington Pass) — several miles of highway from the Cedar Creek Trailhead used for the approach. Carry glacier travel gear (and an ice axe/crampons in early season) for this descent, since it crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine rock rack for 5.9+ terrain; carrying spare cord to back up rappel anchors is recommended by the route's documentation.
rack: Single 9mm rope or thin tag line (two short rappels near Varden Col)
current.pro_needs: Standard rack sized for sustained 5.9+ ridge climbing; supplemental cord/webbing for anchor backups is worth carrying.
current.rope_note: 5.9+ ridge route on Silver Star Mountain (Okanogan); the closest well-documented comparable line (NE Ridge, Grade III 5.9) uses standard glacier-crossing gear plus a light rock rack for scrambling to the summit. A 50-60m single rope covers both glacier travel and short 5th-class ridge pitches.

name: East Ridge
beta: The East Ridge begins with a bergschrund crossing and several pitches (mostly 5.7, often simul-climbed) up vegetated ledges and blocky rock to gain the ridge crest and east face. A 5.8 pitch leads into the route's signature crux: a sustained hand/fist crack (5.9) that nearly every trip report singles out. Above the crux, moderate 4th/low-5th-class climbing continues along an exposed, knife-edged crest to the true summit. The route is graded III, 6 pitches, 800 ft, but many parties describe the full outing — including simul-climbed sections — as feeling more like 8-10 pitches / Grade IV given the long glacier approach and multi-rappel descent.
overview: Widely regarded as one of the best rock routes in the Picket Range and among Fred Beckey's favorite North American climbs. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Dave Collins, and Ed Cooper in October 1958 (weekend of Oct 5), on a second attempt at the then-unclimbed east ridge. The route starts at the base of the south face, gains a col to reach the ridge proper, then follows about 8-10 pitches of mid-5th to 5.9 climbing sustained and exposed, on rock that is loose low down and excellent higher, highlighted by a 30m sustained 5.9 hand-and-fist crack and an airy final low-5th traverse across the summit ridge to the top.

current.approach: This route shares the Goodell Creek trailhead and the same long approach as the West Ridge/South Face routes: the Goodell Creek Trail runs ~4 easy miles along the creek from the trailhead (near the group campground west of Newhalem, off SR-20) to about 1,600 ft, where the last reliable water is found, then a steep, switchback-free climbers' boot path grinds up roughly 3,400-4,000 ft of forested hillside with no water to reach timberline around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above timberline, a rising traverse on meadow, slab, and snow leads to the broad saddle at ~6,000-6,200 ft, with camp typically made just below it in Terror Creek Basin. From camp, the route to the base of the East Ridge continues across glacier-scoured slabs and onto the Terror Glacier beneath Inspiration's South Face — the glacier crossing is low-angle but heavily crevassed, generally with adequate snow bridges in season, so rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear. Unlike the West Ridge and South Face lines, the East Ridge is started by continuing across the glacier below the South Face, crossing the moat or bergschrund toward its eastern end, and working up broken gullies and vegetated ledges, often simul-climbed, to gain the ridge; the sustained, exposed climbing begins once you are on the crest. Total approach is roughly 7 miles and 6,000+ ft of gain from the trailhead to the base of the route, typically consuming most of a full day, and this is consistently rated one of the longer, more strenuous approaches in the North Cascades — budget an early alpine start on summit day given the distance already covered just to reach camp.
approach_variant_names: As for the West Ridge and South Face to the Terror Glacier, then across the glacier below the South Face to the moat under its eastern end
current.descent: There is no established East Ridge descent — the standard way down combines two other routes: parties downclimb/rappel the upper West Ridge crest, then continue down Inspiration's South Face to regain the Terror Glacier, essentially the same descent used by West Ridge climbers (the East Ridge is reported as distinctly poorer, looser rock for descending, so nobody down-climbs it). Parties describe on the order of 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge followed by a scramble to a notch and roughly 9 more rappels down the South Face (about 12-14 total), typically on a single 60-70m rope, using a mix of fixed slings/rap stations of variable quality (back these up) and natural gear anchors. Some parties instead run the full West Ridge on a doubled rope, taking around 7 longer double-rope rappels off natural nut/cam anchors and skipping the separate South Face section. Expect a long free-hanging rappel or two, rockfall-prone traversing stations, and the need to re-rope for glacier travel immediately upon reaching the Terror Glacier at the bottom before reversing the approach back to camp and out the Goodell Creek boot path/trail — this exit is long enough that parties commonly finish it after dark.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack from 0.3 to 3 inches, doubles in the 1-2 inch range (larger hand/fist-sized cams especially useful for the crux crack), six or so smaller stoppers, a mix of alpine draws and double-length runners, plus extra cord/tat for rappel anchors on the West Ridge descent.
rack: Single cam rack .2/.3–3in, doubled in 1-2in and 2-3in
current.pro_needs: Standard alpine trad rack weighted toward hand-to-fist-sized cams for the crux pitch, plus glacier travel gear (crampons, ice axe, rope, crevasse-rescue kit) for the Terror Glacier crossing.
current.rope_note: Verified 2024 trip report beta: crampons, ice axe, single 70m rope, one set of nuts, cams .2-3 with doubles of 2 and 3. Descent is 14 rappels (5 down the upper West Ridge, 9 down the South Face) — bring extra cord for rap anchors.

name: East Ridge
beta: Considered the easiest way up Mount Thomson and the standard descent for the West Ridge as well. After the long PCT approach to Bumblebee Pass and down into the basin, a steep heather-and-talus slope gains an obvious notch (~5,600 ft) on the peak's ESE ridge; from there the route trends left across class 3 terrain to a short, exposed 20-ft class 4 step guarding the true summit, which most parties protect with a rope.
overview: The East Ridge is Mount Thomson's easiest natural line and the standard descent for parties climbing the West Ridge. It's sustained Class 3 scrambling on solid rock with one short, exposed Class 4 chimney (~20 ft) just below the summit. The peak's original 1917 ascent (Joe Hazard and B. French) is generally attributed to an easy east-side line like this one, though no published account gives the exact route taken.

current.approach: From the PCT North Trailhead at I-90 Exit 52 (~3,000 ft), follow the Pacific Crest Trail north through Commonwealth Basin and up onto the Kendall Ridge switchbacks. At roughly 5.5-5.7 miles you reach the Kendall Katwalk, the exposed rock traverse blasted into the cliff band that most parties use as a progress checkpoint. Continue north past Ridge Lake and Gravel/Alaska Lake — the last reliable water before the high basin and ridge — for another 0.3-2 miles to the base of Bumblebee Pass. A short, steep, unmaintained climbers' path (loose tread, care warranted with a pack) climbs to the 5,400 ft pass, then drops down the north side into the open basin directly below Mount Thomson's south face (this basin doubles as the standard camp for West Ridge parties). From the basin, aim for the steep heather-and-talus slope leading to an obvious notch at about 5,600 ft on the East (ESE) Ridge — loose talus and minor route-finding here are the main approach-specific hazards. From the notch, scramble up and traverse left (mostly Class 2-3) along the ridge crest to the base of the final summit block. Total one-way distance from the trailhead to the summit is roughly 8 miles, and the round trip gains about 4,900 ft (the up-and-over at Bumblebee Pass adds extra elevation beyond the net summit height). Expect a long day: parties commonly report 3-5 hours car-to-basin and a full 9-11 hour round trip.
approach_variant_names: PCT to Bumblebee Pass, into the south-face basin, then the heather-and-talus slope to the ESE notch
current.descent: Descent reverses the East Ridge line back to the 5,600 ft notch and down into the basin, then back up and over Bumblebee Pass to rejoin the PCT for the hike out. On the ridge itself, established rappel stations exist at up to three short steps, marked by fixed/fresh webbing and rappel rings threaded on rock horns (not bolted). The crux is a short ~20 ft Class 4 step just below the summit block — most parties either rappel it, rig a handline, or downclimb it if comfortable. One or two additional short rappel/downclimb sections lie higher on the ridge and are optional; confident scramblers downclimb Class 3 terrain there instead of building an anchor. A 30-35m single rope (or a doubled rope) reaches the anchors for all three stations, though at least one pitch has been reported to run close to the limit of a 30m rope, so carrying a 35-40m single rope (or rapping on doubled strands from a 60m) gives more margin. Watch for loose, dirty rock, particularly around the second rappel/downclimb section, and keep parties tight since the ridge is exposed on both sides. Once back at the basin, reclimb roughly 300 ft over Bumblebee Pass before descending to Ridge Lake and the PCT for the return hike to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Little to no protection is placed on this scramble route. Carry a rope and a few slings or rap tat for the final class 4 step, which most parties rappel or handline rather than downclimb.
rack: Small cam rack to 3in for backing up rappel anchors
current.pro_needs: Minimal — this is a scramble route with one short technical step; a rope is optional gear for the final 20-ft class 4 section rather than a true protection system.
bivy: Ridge Lake and Gravel Lake, PCT beyond Kendall Katwalk
current.rope_note: Mostly Class 2 via Bumblebee Pass approach with one exposed ~20 ft Class 4 move near the summit; many parties rope up for this move.

name: East Ridge
beta: From the Castle-Pinnacle col, take the obvious east ridge up Pinnacle. Pitch 1 scrambles mostly 4th-class terrain to a belay ledge at a large dead tree. Pitch 2 is the crux: blocky mid-5th-class climbing with an exposed traverse (an old, unreliable piton is present) to a sandy belay bench that has a fixed rappel anchor dropping the south face. Pitch 3 is mellow terrain to the true summit and is often simul-climbed or soloed by comfortable parties. Loose rock and scree are a serious, persistent concern throughout.
overview: A three-pitch alpine ridge climb up Pinnacle Peak's east side, starting from the saddle between The Castle and Pinnacle Peak. The route follows the obvious east ridge over blocky, sometimes loose rock, with climbing up to 5.5 on the crux second pitch, finishing on easy ground to the summit.

current.approach: From the Reflection Lakes trailhead, follow the maintained Pinnacle Saddle Trail 1.3 mi (~1,000-1,050 ft gain) to the Pinnacle-Plummer saddle. From the saddle, continue on the unmaintained boot path east/behind Pinnacle toward Castle Peak to reach the Castle-Pinnacle col; the east ridge of Pinnacle rises directly from this col. Allow roughly 2-3 hours and about 1,500 ft of gain for this approach segment.
approach_variant_names: Pinnacle Saddle, then east behind Pinnacle to the Castle-Pinnacle col
current.descent: Either rappel from the belay bench atop pitch 2 down the south face on the anchor there, or continue over the summit and descend via the standard south-side scramble route back to Pinnacle Saddle (best if the leader already knows that line) — the scramble descent is blocky downclimbing with comparatively low exposure.
current.detailed_rack: 5-8 double-length runners; 2-4 small-to-mid cams (~0.4-0.75in); a few nuts; single 60m rope (on pitch 3 it may not stretch from the pitch-2 anchor all the way to the true summit, depending on where the anchor is built; the ground there is easy enough that this rarely matters).
current.pro_needs: Protection is thin for the grade — mostly nuts and small-to-mid cams plus extra slings for horns; do not rely on the old fixed piton on pitch 2 as primary protection.
bivy: Reflection Lakes area winter snow camp

name: East Slope
beta: Little more than a walk once the Lucky Pass col is reached — the difficulty of this route lies almost entirely in the approach (creek crossing, steep brushy ridge gain, and a glacier traverse), not the summit scramble itself. Most parties treat it as a 2-3 day backcountry trip out of Colonial Creek Campground.
overview: The East Slope (East Ridge from Lucky Pass) is Primus Peak's standard, easiest line — Class 2-3 rock and moderate glacier travel above a long backcountry approach up Thunder Creek. It's the most commonly described route on the peak, often combined with neighboring Tricouni Peak (8,102 ft) from the same col.

current.approach: Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue about half a mile and leave the maintained trail, dropping steeply to cross Thunder Creek, to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). Expect about 8 1/4 miles and 4,800 ft of gain from the trailhead to this camp, roughly 9 hours with an overnight pack. Note: the footbridge that once crossed Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp is gone, so the crossing is a log jam or a wade — check current park trail conditions before you go.
approach_variant_names: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the East Ridge back to Lucky Pass and descend the same eastern-margin line on the Borealis Glacier used on the ascent, staying off the central icefall. There is no established rappel line; parties without a rope can generally walk this off in good conditions, but carry a rope/pickets in case of deteriorating snow bridges.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for this scramble/glacier route. Parties rope up for the Borealis Glacier crossing near Lucky Pass and carry standard glacier travel gear (rope, pickets, prusiks) — one trip report used two 30m ropes for a party of five.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed; glacier travel gear (rope, pickets/ice screws as needed) covers the crevasse hazard on the Borealis Glacier traverse.
bivy: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
Bivy at toe of Borealis Glacier
current.rope_note: Class 3 max via East Ridge from the Primus-Tricouni Col ('Lucky Pass'); glacier travel required to reach the col - carry ice axe, crampons, and a rope for crevasse rescue on approach.

name: South Route
beta: The South Route climbs East Twin Needle from Crescent Creek Basin by the loose south-facing gullies to the Eye Col, the notch between East and West Twin Needle. Small chockstones low in the gully are scrambled past; the larger ones higher up are fifth class and are usually pitched, and a short scree walk finishes at the col. From the col the route climbs the steep summit block directly above, with a short hand-crack crux near the top that can hold ice early in the season; the summit is small, with a sheer drop to the east. Descend by downclimbing and rappelling back to the Eye Col, then down the south gullies with several short rappels off natural anchors. This is a different climb from the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) put up during the 2003 Southern Pickets enchainment, which is reached along the crest from the east and is not gained from the Eye Col.
overview: East Twin Needle (7,868 ft) is the eastern and slightly lower of the Twin Needles pinnacles in the Southern Pickets, 0.55 mi west of Mount Terror and just east of its taller sister summit, West Twin Needle (7,936 ft). William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg made the first ascent of West Twin Needle on August 17, 1932. East Twin Needle was not climbed on that trip, and its first ascent came later. Composed of solid Skagit gneiss, the pair rises above Crescent Creek Basin near the Mustard Glacier and is almost always climbed as a linked outing from one camp given the shared, multi-day approach. Besides the moderate line described here, East Twin Needle also has a notably harder, more direct East Arête (rated II 5.10a, climbed during the 2003 Southern Picket Range enchainment) and a 2022-established North Buttress ("Thread of Gneiss," 2,000 ft, 5.9, 9 pitches) - be sure you're on the intended, moderate line.

current.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone Access Trailhead off SR-20 near milepost 119 (elev. ~600'). Follow the Goodell Creek Trail, an old forestry roadbed running through open forest along Goodell Creek, for roughly 4-4.5 miles. Near the trail's end, leave the maintained tread at a large cairn marking the start of the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path and ford Terror Creek (can run high with snowmelt in early/mid summer - scout for a safe crossing). From the creek, the route shoots straight up the increasingly brushy crest of 'The Barrier,' a steep, dry ridge with essentially no water until small snowmelt puddles appear around 5,400'. Timberline is reached near 5,600', where travel opens onto slabs and heather in 'Stump Hollow' between the Barrier crest and the Chopping Block. Most parties camp on the Chopping Block ridge (~6,400'), making the car-to-camp day roughly 6-7.5 miles with about 5,800-6,000' of gain - a full, strenuous day, and the crux of the whole trip for many parties (loose talus, fading cairns/flagging, and route-finding through brush make The Barrier notorious for turning parties around). Parties wanting a camp nearer the Needles can instead drop about 200-250' off the ridge crest into Crescent Creek Basin and traverse roughly a mile cross-country (talus, slabs, occasional snow) staying near 5,800', to a camp below Mount Terror at about 6,050' near two streams fed by overhead slabs (reliable water, unlike the Barrier). From this basin camp, descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col and onto the route involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty (this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light) before reaching the col, from which the route climbs East Twin Needle's summit block directly above.
approach_variant_names: Crescent Creek Basin to the Eye Col
current.descent: Most parties reverse the route: downclimb the south-facing gullies back to the Eye Col and continue down into Crescent Creek Basin, a mix of class 4 downclimbing and short rappels off natural anchors (rock horns and slings - no bolted stations reported) on loose rock; expect 1-3 short single-rope rappels depending on snow coverage and the exact gully taken. East Twin Needle is frequently climbed in combination with West Twin Needle as part of a Southern Pickets enchainment; in that case parties continue the ridge west and exit via the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch rather than re-descending the Eye Col gullies. That exit is better documented: two rappels using double 60m ropes are needed below the notch to get past vertical slabs, landing on grass and sloping rock around 6,800'; from there the route continues down a south gully with additional short rappels over vertical rock above a lingering snowfield before regaining Crescent Creek Basin. All anchors encountered on this descent are natural (horns, chockstones, slings) - carry cord/webbing for anchor building and expect to leave gear. From Crescent Creek Basin, reverse the approach: back up and over the Chopping Block ridge, down The Barrier (roughly 4,300' of descent to Terror Creek - loose and brushy, arguably harder in descent than ascent), across Terror Creek, and out the Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Recommended rack includes a single set of BD Camalots from .3 to #2 (gneiss climbing favors cams due to parallel crack systems), a selection of passive protection (wedges/nuts), approximately 10-15 quickdraws, slings, cordelette, and two full-length 60-meter dynamic ropes. Given the gneiss rock type and mixed terrain, emphasis should be placed on camming devices that can handle variable crack widths.
current.pro_needs: The South Route requires solid rock climbing skills at 5.7 grade with competence in multi-pitch trad climbing. Leaders should be experienced at route-finding on complex alpine faces and comfortable with modest class 4 scrambling. Ability to place protection quickly and accurately in shifting rock and gneiss terrain is essential. This is an alpine expedition-style climb requiring self-rescue competence and remote wilderness mountaineering experience.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
current.rope_note: Picket Range alpine rock route by the Eye Col; the hard southeast ridge/face (east arête) is a separate line. Standard alpine rack, glacier approach gear (ice axe/crampons) for Crescent Creek basin approach, 60m rope for multi-pitch rock, plus a second 60m rope for the double-rope rappels if you descend by the Himmelhorn-West Twin Needle notch.

name: East Wilmans Spire
beta: Climbed via the historic 1945 Beckey-Staley line on the spire's southeast side: from the east notch, a short pitch gains a ramp system that is followed up and west, then a final slab/crack pitch (crux) leads to a summit ledge. Two short raps and a downclimb return to the notch. The rock is loose in places (especially early in a pitch or on the east aspect), so care with hand/footholds and rope management is important on this wandering line.
overview: A short, moderate alpine rock route up the easternmost of the three Wilmans Spires, a needle of volcanic breccia dividing Glacier Basin from Seventy-Six Basin, ending on a famously tiny, table-top summit with commanding views over the Monte Cristo group.

current.approach: From Granite Falls, drive the paved Mountain Loop Highway east roughly 31 miles (passing the Verlot Public Service Center) to Barlow Pass, where pavement ends and the Monte Cristo Road is gated to motor vehicles. Hike or mountain-bike the flat, gated road about 4 miles along the South Fork Sauk River to the historic Monte Cristo townsite (a washout near the Twin Bridges area may require a ford or log crossing of the river). From the townsite, pick up the Glacier Basin Trail and follow it a short distance before leaving the trail to climb a steep talus/scree gully - snow-covered and firmer in early season, loose and increasingly rockfall-prone once melted out by mid/late summer - up to the east notch/col below East Wilmans Spire, where the roped climbing begins.
approach_variant_names: Glacier Basin Trail to the east notch
current.descent:
From the summit, make two single-rope rappels down the line of ascent. The first is short, off the three-piton anchor on the summit block, and lands at the slung rock at the top of pitch 2; the second takes you down pitch 2 to the top of pitch 1.

From there most parties do not rappel again: they climb back over the 20-ft 5.5 crack that pitch 1 downclimbs on the way in, then downclimb to the east notch. That reversal is made unroped with about a thousand feet of exposure below and is the most committing move of the descent, though it goes more easily backwards than it looks. Some parties instead make a third rappel straight down into the gully from the top of pitch 1, which is why recorded rappel counts here differ between two and three.

From the notch, downclimb the approach gully — glissading remaining snow where present, or picking carefully through loose talus and scree later in the season — back to the Glacier Basin Trail, then retrace the approach through Monte Cristo townsite to Barlow Pass.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack is sufficient: a set of nuts and cams (small to about 2 inches, with a #2 Camalot noted as particularly useful), optionally a few hexes, plus extra slings/draws to manage rope drag on the wandering line. Two old fixed pins protect the crux crack on P3 but should be backed up with gear where possible.
current.pro_needs: Standard light alpine trad rack - nuts and cams up to roughly 2 inches - protects all three pitches adequately; the crux P3 crack has two old fixed pins as well. Plenty of slings help on the meandering ramp/corner terrain to reduce rope drag.
bivy: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road

name: Easy Getaway
beta: Stellar rock quality with excellent crack and corner climbing plus slab sections; because of the demanding approach, parties typically have the route to themselves. Use 'Zebra Corner' as the key landmark throughout the climb to confirm you're on route - it can seep water early season. Blake Herrington's Cascades Rock topo is the recommended reference since the wall has more variations than are documented online.
overview: An 8-pitch, 800-ft moderate-to-sustained trad line up excellent crack-and-corner granite on the left side of Cutthroat Wall, capped by a standout 100-ft right-facing corner near the top.

current.approach: This is a distinct approach from the one used for Cutthroat Peak, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail. For Cutthroat Wall, start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483 from the Cutthroat Trailhead kiosk. After a short distance on the main trail, leave it via a cairned path that cuts into the forest, then follow cairns and a climbers' path (roughly 1.5-2 miles, 45 min-2 hrs total) through brush and talus, trending toward the buttress, to reach the base of Cutthroat Wall.
approach_variant_names: Cutthroat Creek trail #483 from the Cutthroat Lake trailhead
current.descent: The descent has real potential to ruin your day if you don't study it beforehand. From the topout, reach the notch marked by a slung horn/tree between the westernmost and higher central buttress, make one rappel (two 60m ropes, since a single 60m can fall short) over a chockstone tunnel to a dirty ramp with a small cave, then find the upward-trending gully/ledge system on skier's left (not the loose gully directly below) and follow it around back to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Cams: doubles from tips to #2, plus a single #3 and single #4. Stoppers: single set.
current.pro_needs: A doubled small-to-medium cam rack (tips through #2) with single #3 and #4 for occasional wider sections, plus a single stopper set; minimal fixed protection.
bivy: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby

name: East Ridge (Inspiration Glacier)
beta: From the Eldorado Creek trailhead, a steep boot trail gains a talus basin near 4,000 ft; open slopes lead to a high camp between roughly 5,400 and 7,800 ft near the Eldorado Glacier margin. From camp, rope up and cross the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers, gain 'the Gap' on the lower East Ridge, then follow the exposed snow crest to the small summit.
overview: Eldorado Peak is the glittering centerpiece of its namesake icecap, and the East Ridge route over the Inspiration Glacier is the classic ascent, famous for its airy summit snow arête. The climb travels across a broad, gentle glacier before narrowing to a knife-edge crest of snow that drops away dramatically on both sides to the true summit. It is a moderate but spectacular glacier mountaineering outing in the heart of the North Cascades.

current.approach: Start at the Eldorado Trailhead (Eldorado Creek Climbers' Path) at mile 20 of Cascade River Road, elevation ~2,100 ft (pit toilet at the parking area). From the parking area, backtrack downstream about 90 feet on the road and look for a log or a clump of three trees spanning the Cascade River — cross here (this crossing can be exposed and slick when wet or in high water; a rope/handline is prudent for less experienced parties), then walk roughly 100 feet perpendicular to the river to pick up the climbers' trail. The path climbs steeply through heavy timber, gaining about 1,500 ft before breaking out onto talus. Follow cairns and flagging up the boulder field, staying climber's right to avoid an unnecessary crossing of Eldorado Creek, until the talus eases into the open, beautiful alpine Eldorado Creek Basin (a common first camp at roughly 5,400–5,600 ft, ~3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead). From the basin, climb up onto a rocky ridge at about 6,100 ft, then drop a few hundred feet on the far side into Roush Creek Basin (an alternate/second camp at 6,100–6,400 ft, with reliable running water). From Roush Basin, ascend broken talus and slabs onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier and continue up moderate glacier slopes to a high camp near 7,500–7,800 ft on the Eldorado–Inspiration Glacier saddle, with views of Moraine Lake, McAllister Glacier and Klawatti Glacier. Rope up for glacier travel here — the Eldorado and Inspiration Glaciers carry real crevasse hazard, worse as the day warms; parties have broken through hidden snow-bridged creek channels even in the lower basins in spring. From high camp, cross the mostly flat Inspiration Glacier aiming for the low gap on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, then follow the ridge/snow arete up to the base of the summit knife-edge. Total gain is roughly 6,700–6,800 ft trailhead-to-summit; guided parties budget 5–7 hours to high camp and another 3–5 hours (6–9 hours total on summit day) from camp to the top.
approach_variant_names: Eldorado Creek climbers' path to Inspiration Glacier high camp
Late-spring snow cover (skis or boots)
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the exposed, corniced knife-edge summit ridge (in certain conditions a very thin edge with steep — 40–45°+ — flanks; ice axe and crampons essentially mandatory, and rope/running-belay technique is common for less experienced members), continue down through the gap in the lower East Ridge, then rope up again to cross the Inspiration Glacier and descend the Eldorado Glacier back to Roush Basin, over the intervening ridge into Eldorado Creek Basin, and down the boulder field and timbered climbers' trail to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappels are used on the standard route; multiple trip reports and guide-service itineraries describe the descent purely in terms of downclimbing and reversing glacier travel, and note that some parties have even skied the ridge and glaciers in spring conditions rather than roping for rappels. Watch for softening snow bridges and increasing crevasse hazard on the glaciers later in the day (afternoon descents in summer are notably less secure than an early-morning ascent), and for the knife-edge becoming icy/firm late-season, which can make the downclimb more consequential and prompt some parties to belay short sections rather than rappel them.
current.detailed_rack: A 30 to 60m glacier rope and a couple of pickets. No rock gear is needed.
current.pro_needs: Protection is limited to pickets on the summit arête and standard glacier-travel anchors. The route is about snow and glacier skills rather than rock protection.

name: Northwest Couloir / Eldorado Glacier
beta: Approach via the East Ridge glacier track to a rappel notch between Eldorado Peak and Dean's Spire (~8,100 ft), rappel into the west-facing cirque, then climb the couloir (~1,000 ft, 7,800–8,800 ft) on snow, neve, or ice depending on conditions — steps to 70–80° — to join the upper East Ridge.
overview: The Northwest Ice Couloir splits the northwest face of Eldorado above the wild Marble Creek Cirque, offering 2-3 long pitches (often simul-climbed) up the couloir to a flat shoulder just below the summit's famous knife-edge ridge — a steeper, more technical alternative to the standard East Ridge, reached via a long and fairly complex glaciated traverse around the mountain.

current.approach: Same trailhead and lower approach as the East Ridge: Eldorado Trailhead at Cascade River Road mile 20 (~2,100 ft), cross the Cascade River via the log/three-tree crossing about 90 ft downstream of the parking area, then climb the steep timbered climbers' trail into a dry boulderfield (roughly to 4,500 ft) and on into Eldorado Creek Basin. From there, continue as for the East Ridge over the Roush Divide and up the Eldorado Glacier, then trend toward the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col on the mountain's northwest side to reach the wild Marble Creek Cirque, with views of Dorado Needle and Early Morning Spire. The approach to this face is longer and more involved than the East Ridge approach — a long, somewhat complicated route across glaciated and crevassed terrain, so rope up for the glacier sections. High camp is typically established either in Eldorado Creek/Roush Creek Basin or higher at the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier site (~7,500–7,600 ft). One recorded ascent (climbing from the trailhead in a single push) took roughly 5 hours to reach the couloir's base; that party also used a shortcut of a belayed downclimb (~35 m) and two 30-meter rappels down a snow/rock gully near the Eldorado–Dean's Spire col to drop directly to within about 100 yards of the couloir, which meaningfully shortens the standard glacier traverse but is a variation, not the only way in — most parties simply continue glacier travel around to the couloir's base at about 7,800 ft. Hazards on approach: crevasses on the Eldorado/Inspiration Glaciers, a long featureless glacier crossing that can be disorienting in whiteout, and the optional gully downclimb/rappel shortcut is itself exposed snow-and-rock terrain.
approach_variant_names: Rappel off the ice cap into the Marble Creek cirque, then the couloir splitting the northwest face
current.descent: From the summit, do not reverse the couloir — descend via the standard East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier route: downclimb the knife-edge summit ridge, drop through the gap in the lower East Ridge, rope up and cross the Inspiration Glacier, then descend the Eldorado Glacier back toward Roush Basin and Eldorado Creek Basin, finishing on the timbered climbers' trail back to the Cascade River crossing and trailhead (see the East Ridge route for full detail). This is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappels required on the descent itself — one party even skied the knife-edge ridge and glacier on the way down. Rappelling comes up on this route only on the approach/entry into the couloir, not on the summit descent: one party used a 40-meter rappel off the Inspiration Glacier side to drop into the couloir's gully system, anchored on two pitons with some newish tat, and noted a full 60m rope would get a party through everything in one rappel rather than needing to downclimb the remainder — but again, this is describing getting into the route, not descending from the summit. Because the descent is the shared East Ridge walk-off, treat glacier crevasse hazard and knife-edge icing exactly as on that route, and carry a rope for the glacier crossings regardless of whether any rappelling was used higher on the mountain.
current.detailed_rack: A few ice screws, a couple of pickets, and a glacier rope.
current.pro_needs: The couloir takes pickets and the occasional screw where ice forms; the glacier uses standard travel anchors. Protection is sparse, so confident steep-snow technique is essential.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: North Ridge
beta: From high camp, descend the Inspiration Glacier to the notch used as the NW Ice Couloir rappel point, then climb steep snow onto the North Ridge proper. The route follows generally solid rock on the ridge's eastern aspect with good friction and incut holds, offering minimal exposure toward the glacier side but dramatic exposure to the west. Near the top, parties can finish directly up steeper ice/rock or join the classic East Ridge finish to the summit.
overview: A shorter, 800-ft moderate rock route on solid golden granite on the eastern aspect of the North Ridge, offering a good introduction to Eldorado's alpine rock above the standard glacier approach.

current.approach: Same approach as the East Ridge to high camp on the Inspiration Glacier, then cross the Inspiration Glacier around the east end of the East Ridge and traverse the glacier on the mountain's north side at about 8,100 ft to the NW Ice Couloir notch at the base of the North Ridge.
approach_variant_names: Down the Inspiration Glacier to the ice-couloir notch, then snow onto the crest
current.descent: Return down the same ridge system to the notch and back to camp on the Inspiration Glacier; parties who finish via the East Ridge instead descend that ridge's knife-edge back to camp.
current.detailed_rack: Light rock rack for 5.7 terrain plus a couple of ice screws for the upper snow/ice sections.
rack: Standard alpine rock rack (cams/nuts) for 5.7 terrain - exact sizes undocumented
Ice axe, crampons, pickets, glacier travel gear for the approach/upper mountain
current.pro_needs: Standard rock protection to 5.7; a small number of ice screws if finishing the ice-direct variation.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
current.rope_note: Confirmed as Eldorado Peak's Main Peak North Ridge: follows the easiest line on clean, solid rock, mostly the east side of the ridge, ending below the summit pinnacle; protection is just a standard alpine rack. Steep snow on the NE Face means glacier travel gear is needed for the approach/upper mountain in addition to the rock rack.

name: West Arete
beta: First climbed in 1969, the West Arete follows the crest of Eldorado's west face for about 19 pitches (including 3 long simul pitches). The lower section is loose 5.6 scrambling through a steep open chimney; the middle section has confusing routefinding through sandy, loose gullies (5.0-5.7) with relentless exposure; the crux is a set of rocky towers finishing in an old-school 5.8 face traverse protected by a single in-situ piton; the upper section continues with chimney climbing and more 5.0-5.7 pitches before three long, loose simul pitches lead to the summit. Most parties treat it as a full multi-day outing: a day to approach, a long day to climb (historically up to ~17 hours round-trip from the East Ridge base camp), and a day to exit.
overview: Perhaps the most spectacular alpine rock climb in the North Cascades — rises nearly 3,000 feet of continuous rock from glacier to summit. Only climbed a few times per season by very competent parties.

current.approach: Start at the Eldorado Creek trailhead on Cascade River Road, follow the climbers' trail up Eldorado Creek into the Roush Creek basin, camp near the base of the East Ridge (about 7,500 ft), then cross the Inspiration and McAllister glaciers to Dorado Needle Col and make a loose fourth-class downclimb into the Marble Creek cirque, traversing to the toe of the arete near 6,000 ft. Typically a 3-day trip (approach day, climb day, exit day); the first roughly 800 ft of climbing is Class 4 before harder 5th-class sections.
approach_variant_names: Over the ice cap to Dorado Needle Col, then down into Marble Creek Cirque
current.descent: From the summit, descend the East Ridge — most parties find this significantly easier and more straightforward than downclimbing the loose West Arete — then return to camp via the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier.
current.detailed_rack: Single set of cams from about .2-3 in, doubles from .5-1 in, a set of nuts, and a 60-70m single rope, plus full glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach.
current.pro_needs: Protection is generally adequate on the lower/middle 5.6-5.7 terrain but sparse and old-school at the 5.8 crux face traverse, which relies on a single fixed piton.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Elephant Butte Standard Route (Stetattle/Sourdough Ridge)
beta: From the Diablo trailhead, the maintained Sourdough Mountain Trail is followed to about 4,300-4,400 ft before leaving the trail on an unmarked climber's path to reach the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge. From there it's an extended, largely trail-less ridge walk (with a short class 3 step near a saddle) toward Elephant Butte. The peak itself presents an obstacle: a short overhung 5th-class move goes more or less directly over it (not recommended with an overnight pack), while most parties instead drop well off the ridge and traverse below/around the peak through brush and mossy micro-cliffs before regaining the ridge crest beyond it. Most climbers do this as part of a multi-day traverse into or out of the Southern Pickets rather than as a dedicated objective, though a very long single-day round trip from Diablo is feasible for fit, fast parties.
overview: A long, mostly non-technical ridge approach and scramble to Elephant Butte via the Sourdough Mountain Trail and the open Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge crest. The crux is not technical climbing but a short, exposed, brush-and-cliff obstacle immediately below the summit that most parties bypass rather than climb directly.

current.approach: Drive State Route 20 (North Cascades Highway) to milepost 126 and turn off at the sign for the village of Diablo, a Seattle City Light company town. Park near the river across from the domed swimming pool; the Sourdough Mountain Trail begins immediately behind the pool building (roughly 890-900 ft). Follow the trail as it switchbacks steeply through forest. At an unmarked junction around 4,300-4,400 ft, leave the maintained trail and head up onto the open crest of Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge (roughly 6,500 ft) rather than continuing to the Sourdough Mountain Lookout; if you reach the Sourdough Creek crossing and open views of Diablo Lake, you have gone past the turn-off. From the ridge crest, continue along the mostly open, trail-less ridge toward Elephant Butte.
approach_variant_names: Sourdough Mountain Trail to the Stetattle Ridge crest
current.descent: From the summit, retrace the approach: regain the ridge crest above the Elephant Butte bypass terrain, then follow the open ridge back toward the Sourdough Mountain Trail junction (around 6,500 ft, then the junction at 4,300-4,400 ft). Drop onto the maintained trail and switchback down through forest to the trailhead at Diablo. Parties using this as a through-route to the Southern Pickets instead continue along the ridge system toward Pioneer Ridge/McMillan Creek and the Pickets rather than returning to Diablo.
current.detailed_rack: No rock protection needed for the mountaineering route (Class 2-3 scrambling bypasses the Class 5 crux). However, many groups carry lightweight trad rack (slings, runners) to set up safety on steep snow traverses or if a group member needs additional security on exposed terrain.
current.pro_needs: No fixed or placed protection is used on this route — it is off-trail hiking/scrambling rather than roped climbing. An ice axe is useful for lingering early-season snow patches on the ridge; some parties carry light rope/webbing for confidence on the class 3 step, though it is not standard practice.
bivy: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
current.rope_note: Standard route is an off-trail ridge/talus approach via Sourdough/Stetattle Ridge with short class 3 rock steps and snowfield crossings; no technical rock rope needed.

name: Ellation
beta: Named for the daughter, Ella, of one of the first ascensionists. Pitch 1 is a bolted groove; pitches 2-3 mix flakes, thin cracks, seams, and steep friction (the mental crux); pitches 4-7 climb knobby, well-bolted face and corner terrain up to sustained 5.10; pitch 8 finishes on a steep juggy face into a flaring corner at 5.11a (or 5.10 with a point of aid). Protection mixes bolts with natural gear throughout — most pitches are partially bolted.
overview: An 8-pitch, roughly 800 ft outing up the best rock on Mamie Peak's center buttress: three pitches of techy slab lead into five sustained, exposed pitches of face, friction, and crack climbing to a 5.11a crux (or 5.10 A0 alternative).

current.approach: From I-5 Exit 255, drive SR-542 (Mt. Baker Highway) east about 46 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) and follow it about 5.3 miles to the road-end Hannegan Pass Trailhead. Mamie Peak's tiered granite walls stand directly above. Walk the Hannegan Pass Trail a few minutes to a clearing below a large white boulder perched high on the slope, then leave the trail on a faint, brushy climbers' path up a gully, a dry creekbed and steep woods to the base of the wall: about an hour and 1,200 ft of gain.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass Trail to the Ellation crag
current.descent:
Rappel the line of ascent on a single 70m rope used doubled. The descent is not one continuous rappel line and does not map onto the pitches: five rappels bring you down the main wall to a gear belay at its toe, then you downscramble a 3rd/4th-class gully to the big treed ledge, then three more rappels reach the ground. Seven of the eight are too long for a 60m rope, and the last is 115 ft — the whole reach of a doubled 70 — so knot the ends.

Two stations need naming in advance. The rappel down pitch 6 is where ropes jam: a crack at the top of the ramp catches the pull, and parties have had to re-climb the pitch to free it. Clip the pull strand through a leaver biner on the second bolt below that station and it stops being a problem. And the station off the big treed ledge is a tree on slings, roughly 30-40 ft to climber's left of the top of pitch 3 — the only anchor on the route without fixed metal, so inspect what you find.

From the base, retrace the brushy climbers' path down through timber and mossy slabs to the Hannegan Pass Trail and out to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack from small cams (red X4/C3-size) up to #1, plus single #2 and #3; offset cams reportedly work well on the seam pitches (especially pitch 3). Bring at least 10 quickdraws/slings for the well-bolted face pitches.
current.pro_needs: A medium rack to 3" with doubles of fingers-to-tight-hand sizes covers the trad placements; most pitches are partially bolted, so 10+ draws are also needed.
bivy: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

name: Ellen Pea
beta: A ground-up effort by two Spokane climbers over several days across a few seasons, completed in 2009. Excellent, squeaky-clean granite throughout, with a well-bolted crux pitch of pocket climbing and a steep exit from the cave regarded by many parties as the route's hardest pitch. The large Supercave itself offers a natural mid-route rest/shelter.
overview: The wall's original modern free line: a sustained 7-pitch 5.11c up the right side of M&M Wall, intersecting the huge Supercave feature at mid-height — one of the most popular and (relatively) easiest routes at the crag.

current.approach: M&M Wall, also known as Supercave Wall for the tennis-court-sized cave crossing the cliff at mid-height, is one of the largest roadside walls at Washington Pass. Park at a pullout near milepost 166 on SR-20, about 3 miles east of the hairpin turns below Washington Pass. From the highway, head directly uphill (west, away from the creek) toward the talus at the base of the Supercave gully, following it up and briefly left before rejoining the gully; it takes roughly 1 hour to reach the lower ledge and about 1 hour 10 minutes to reach the upper ledge and base of the longer routes.
approach_variant_names: Supercave gully to the upper ledge
current.descent: Descend via rappel using two ropes; expect some diagonal-rappel maneuvering to stay on anchors, or traverse off to a 3rd-class ramp partway down. Figure roughly an hour from the summit/top of the route back to the base.
current.detailed_rack: Double cams from tips-sized up through #2 BD, a standard set of wires, and extra extendable draws/long runners (particularly useful through the cave section to cut rope drag).
current.pro_needs: Well protected for a route of its grade — the crux pitch is well-bolted with pocket climbing — but standard trad gear covers the remaining pitches; extendable draws help manage drag through the wandering cave exit.
bivy: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: This is the generic 'easiest route' taken by nearly every party that visits Emerald Peak, almost always as a side-summit from a basin camp shared with Cardinal and/or Saska Peak. It is described consistently as: gain a basin around 6,800-6,900 ft below the Cardinal-Emerald saddle, cross talus/scree to the base of a broad gully, climb the gully (moderate snow early season, loose scree/rock later) to a notch in the summit ridge, then turn and scramble class 2-3 rock (only a very short stretch of class 3 near the top) to the summit. This line has no formal name; 'Southeast Ridge' describes the ridge/notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just SE of Emerald.
overview: Emerald Peak (8,422 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Chelan Mountains, edged out only by Cardinal Peak (8,590 ft, 1.1 mi SE).
