Saska Peak sits just 0.66 mi west-southwest across a narrow basin, and the two peaks — plus nearby Pinnacle Mountain and Cardinal — are commonly linked into a multi-day 'Entiat/Chelan Slam' backpack-and-scramble trip out of the North Fork Entiat valley. The summit block is split into a slightly-higher north summit and a lower south summit about 100 ft away across more steeply-inclined slab; despite the peak's intimidating broad-sided look from a distance, erosion has opened a moderate class 2-3 line up the southeast side. First ascent by William A. Long, 1937.

current.approach: Start at the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead (~3,940 ft) at the end of Forest Road 5606, off Entiat River Road. Take the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437, which follows the North Fork Entiat River upstream through burned/downed timber from past wildfires — expect deadfall requiring detours over, under, or around logs in the lower miles, and a river/creek crossing (Grouse Creek, via a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or a deteriorating footbridge depending on year and washout status) a few miles in. The trail climbs gently through forest, passing the Fern Lake Trail (#1436) junction at about mile 6.1 (roughly 1,300 ft of gain from the trailhead). Continue upvalley; around mile 7 the North Fork Entiat trail turns sharply east/right and switchbacks about a half mile up to its end at the junction with the Pyramid Mountain Trail (#1433) near 6,600 ft. Above this point the maintained trail effectively ends and the route goes cross-country: leave the trail here (or slightly before, depending on snow cover — the tread can be hard to follow once patchy snow sets in above ~4,800 ft in early season) and angle west/southwest, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald Peak. A good camp/staging flat sits around 7,000–7,100 ft in the open basin below Cardinal's north-middle saddle, convenient for both Emerald and neighboring Cardinal/Saska. From this basin, drop 200–300 ft to skirt cliff bands, then regain a 6,900 ft basin south of Emerald Peak. Cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully into the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, which feeds the southeast side of Emerald's summit ridge — this is the start of the southeast ridge scramble proper. Water is reliably available along the North Fork Entiat River and its tributaries for the first ~7 miles but is scarce above the basin, so tank up before leaving the valley bottom. Total one-way distance to the base of the climbing is roughly 9–10 miles with about 3,200–3,400 ft of the route's total gain covered by the time you reach the upper basin, leaving a shorter, steeper final push to the ridge and summit.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
Emerald Park and Milham Pass from Lucerne
current.descent: Descend by reversing the southeast ridge/gully line used on ascent: downclimb class 2–3 terrain from the summit block back to the notch in the upper basin between Saska and Emerald, then follow the gully back down to the 6,900 ft basin and re-cross the shoulder to the camp flat near 7,000–7,100 ft. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors or rappel stations are reported on this route, and parties climbing the Saska–Emerald–Cardinal group describe simul-downclimbing or careful scrambling rather than rappelling, since the class 2-3 terrain generally isn't steep or exposed enough to require rope work. The main descent hazards are loose, blocky rock in the gully (rockfall risk onto parties below, and ankle-turning talus/scree lower down) and, in early season, moderate snow in the gully requiring an ice axe and possibly crampons — parties have noted lingering snow patches into summer. From the basin, retrace the cross-country line back to the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction and descend the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 the full ~9 miles back to the trailhead, watching footing on the same deadfall and creek crossings encountered on the way in (a crampon-related slip near the final miles has been reported, so stay attentive even on the "easy" trail portion when fatigued). If any party member is uncomfortable with the exposure in the gully/notch section, a short hand-line or single rappel off natural gear (block/horn) could reasonably be rigged, but this is not standard practice for the route.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is used on this scramble — it is unroped class 2-3 terrain for essentially all parties.
current.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble route; a rope is not carried by documented parties.
bivy: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble; hands-on-rock but no rope typically carried. Ice axe recommended early season.

name: West Route
beta: Despite the peak's craggy appearance suggesting no easy line exists, erosion has cut a class 3 gully/weakness up the west side that is catalogued as a named, rated route (skill 2 / fitness 2). It tops out on a summit divided into two high points roughly 100 ft apart — the north summit is slightly higher, and the south summit has notably more exposure, with a steep slab dropping toward the East Face. Access is via the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 from the standard trailhead, or alternately via the Emerald Park Trail #1230 starting from Lucerne on Lake Chelan's shore (a boat-access approach).
overview: A distinct, dedicated line on the peak: an easy class 3 scramble to Emerald's summit block (three summit points show from below, and the middle one is the goal) via an erosion-carved gully on the peak's west side, reached from the same North Fork Entiat trailhead (or alternately from Lake Chelan via the Emerald Park Trail).

current.approach: Primary approach: from Entiat, drive Entiat River Road ~32.5 miles to Forest Road 5606, then ~3 switchbacking miles to the North Fork Entiat Trailhead (~3,940 ft); hike NF Entiat River Trail #1437 up-valley and leave the trail to gain the west-side gully below Emerald's summit block. Alternate approach: from Lucerne on Lake Chelan (reached by boat/ferry), hike the Emerald Park Trail #1230 up into Emerald Park and approach the peak's west side from there. In mid-June the North Fork Entiat trail had many fallen trees, the first three to four miles run through burned forest with little shade, and snow patches covered the trail from about 6,600 to 6,900 ft. By early July the trail had been cleared of most blowdowns, though a few logs still needed climbing over, and the basin below the peak had plenty of water and no snow crossings.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Entiat Trail #1437 to the meadow camp
Emerald Park trail from Lucerne
current.descent: Downclimb from the summit block back through the class 3 gully on the west side, taking care on the steep slab near the south summit and the East Face exposure; regain the basin and retrace either the North Fork Entiat or Emerald Park Trail approach.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack — unroped class 3 scrambling.
current.pro_needs: None — rope is not used by documented parties on this line.
bivy: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail

name: Enchantment Enchainment
beta: Peak order and exact lines are up to the party; the loop below runs west to east. Stuart: from the Stuart Lake valley climb slopes toward Long Pass, then steep snow to a notch at about 7,950 ft on the northwest face; drop slightly, traverse snow to a gully that shortcuts onto the upper West Ridge (continuous snow early season, with 3rd class rock beside it), then follow the West Ridge to the summit. The West Ridge is a notorious route-finding trap that benights parties climbing it for the first time, so know the line before you go. Sherpa: descend the upper Cascadian Couloir and cut east to the Stuart-Sherpa col (a short 4th class downclimb on the way), then climb Sherpa's West Ridge, keeping left of the steeper cracks on easier ground. Leave Sherpa by the north side: a short 4th/5th class downclimb, then trend skier's left through a scrambly gully to a large vegetated ledge near 8,100 ft, and on down a broader gully to about 7,200 ft. Sherpa to Argonaut: a long, time-consuming traverse across high granite slabs and goat paths to Argonaut's south-side gullies; the alternative is to drop to the valley trail and climb back up. Argonaut: ascend the southern gullies on easy ground to just below the east ridge, with a short easy-fifth-class step to the summit; descend by rappel down the east face. Colchuck and Dragontail: gain the Colchuck-Dragontail col and tag each summit by its scramble from the col, then descend to Aasgard Pass. The Core: from Aasgard Pass continue into the upper Enchantment basin for Little Annapurna (a walk-up from the basin), McClellan Peak (loose scrambling), then Enchantment Peak via Prusik Pass (talus, with a 4th class summit pillar; it has two summits of similar height, so tag both if in doubt) and finally Cannon Mountain from the Enchantment side.
overview: A car-to-car loop from the Stuart Lake trailhead that links the nine tallest summits of the Enchantments area: Mount Stuart, Sherpa, Argonaut, Colchuck, Dragontail, Little Annapurna, McClellan, Enchantment Peak and Cannon Mountain. It is about 27 miles and roughly 18,000 ft of gain over steep snow, several pitches of low-fifth-class rock and a very large amount of loose 3rd and 4th class scrambling. It is an enchainment rather than a true ridge traverse: the line leaves the crest wherever easier ground links one summit to the next.

current.approach: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the Stuart Lake trail up Mountaineer Creek through old burn toward Stuart Lake. Beyond the lake leave the trail and climb the slopes, then steep snow, to the notch on Stuart's northwest face that gives the shortcut onto the upper West Ridge. The West Ridge is normally approached from the south, so this north-side access sees little traffic; expect snow in the notch and gully well into summer.
current.descent: Two ways out from Cannon. The direct line drops north off Cannon straight toward the Stuart Lake trail and the trailhead: roughly 5,000 vertical ft of loose dirt, talus and cliff bands in the upper half, then steep brush and unmapped cliff bands in the lower 2,000 ft, which is slow and miserable, especially in the dark. The longer but known alternative is to return across the Core to Aasgard Pass and descend to Colchuck Lake and the trail back to the trailhead.
rack: A few small to medium cams
Cord for backing up rappel anchors
current.pro_needs: Light: a handful of pieces for short fifth-class steps and to back up rappel anchors.
current.rope_note: Some parties solo it, but the Argonaut descent is a rappel route and Stuart's West Ridge and Sherpa both have fifth-class steps, so most parties carry a light rope.

name: South Gully
beta: From a camp in the Core Enchantment Zone, or straight off Aasgard Pass on a long day, cross the lakes basin and leave it between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun, heading north over talus to the gully on the south side directly below the northeast summit. The going is class 2-3 with a few exposed spots and good holds, and a short third-class scramble up the south side finishes on the northeast summit, a flat block about 6 ft square and the true high point. The southwest summit, roughly 1,500 ft away along the crest, is a narrow, very exposed fourth-class (some say low fifth) fin and is not part of this route; the Prusik Pass east-ridge route is the other way onto the northeast summit.
overview: Enchantment Peak (8,538 ft) is the granite high point of the Core Enchantments, rising on the ridge between Prusik Peak (NE) and Dragontail Peak/Aasgard Pass (SW), within the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The peak actually has two summits about 1,500 ft apart and of nearly equal height: the NE summit is the traditionally recognized true high point — a short, fun class 3 scramble to a roughly 6x6 ft flat block — while the SW summit is a narrow ~1-ft-wide, 6-ft-long granite fin reached only by an exposed class 4 (some say low 5th class) scramble that most parties skip. This route reaches the NE summit from the south, crossing the Core basin from the Aasgard Pass side to a gully below that summit; it does not visit the technical SW pinnacle.

current.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (elev. ~3,400 ft) on FS Road 7601 off Icicle Road. Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (Trail #1599) south up the Mountaineer Creek valley through Douglas-fir/subalpine forest, crossing Mountaineer Creek on sturdy footbridges; the grade is moderate for the first 2.5 miles (about 1,500 ft gain) to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail — go left/uphill. From the junction the trail steepens and grows rockier for another 1.5 miles to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and ~2,280 ft from the TH, lake at 5,570 ft) — the last reliable, easy water source before the high basin. Boulder-hop/skirt the lake's west shore to the boulder field at its south end and the base of Aasgard Pass, a steep, unmaintained talus-and-boulder gully with only faint tread and cairns; it gains roughly 2,000–2,200 ft in under 1.25 miles to the pass (~7,800–7,841 ft) — this is the single biggest approach hazard on the route: loose, shifting rock with real rockfall risk onto parties below, and in early season the gully holds snow/ice that turns it into a steep, exposed snow climb. From the pass, drop gently into the upper Enchantment core basin past Isolation Lake, then traverse cross-country (use-paths and cairns, no maintained trail) through the Tranquil/Perfection/Sigrun/Reginleif lakes tarn cluster toward the Enchantment Peak massif; this route leaves the basin directly between Lake Reginleif and Lake Sigrun and climbs talus to the gully on the peak's south side below the northeast summit, avoiding the longer detour via Prusik Pass. This upper section is class 2–3 talus and slab with sustained exposure in spots; snow lingering into summer can make it markedly harder and is best avoided when icy (some parties instead take the longer, mellower line via Prusik Pass in spring conditions). The route enters fragile alpine terrain in the wilderness's day-use/permit core zone — stay on rock or snow and avoid cutting across meadow or heather. One-way distance to the summit is roughly 7.5–8 miles with about 5,100 ft of net rise from trailhead to summit; counting the drop into the basin and the reclimb to Aasgard Pass on the way out, the round trip comes to roughly 6,650 ft of gain for a car-to-car push (long day; many split it with a camp near Colchuck or in the core zone under permit).
approach_variant_names: Aasgard Pass and the core basin to the south side
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line. This route tops out on the northeast summit, which a 2023 survey confirms is the true high point, and its descent is a walk-off: downclimb the short, loose 3rd-class gully off the summit plateau — the same step you came up — then reverse the cross-country traverse back through the Reginleif/Sigrun tarn basin to the top of Aasgard Pass. Downclimbing Aasgard Pass is the descent's main hazard: steep, loose talus that's arguably harder to descend than ascend — plunge-step or downclimb deliberately and stay off snow you can't see the run-out on. Do not glissade the snow-filled sections of Aasgard Pass; several serious and fatal accidents have occurred there from glissaders sliding into hidden moats and sub-snow meltwater channels, especially in early-to-mid season. From the base of the pass, follow the Colchuck Lake shoreline and the Colchuck Lake Trail / Stuart Lake Trail back to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb route overall — no established rappels on the standard line.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear is needed for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: There is no protectable climbing on the easiest line; movement is unroped scrambling. The demands are basic route-finding and comfort on exposed third-class blocks rather than any gear.
bivy: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road

name: Ephemeral
beta: Starts on water-polished rock, pulls a small roof, works through a thin crux, then hangs on through a leftward traverse on good holds to the bolted anchors.
overview: The four-star testpiece of the crag: a steep, technical single-pitch sport line up water-polished granite on the left side of the Ice Box right side wall.

current.approach: From the large pullout at the SR-20 hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, follow the climbers' path uphill toward Spire Gully and the Quicksilver Slabs, then cut right into the dry creek bed below the chasm. Cross left beneath the first slab and scramble 3rd-class ground up the left edge of the smooth, slippery slabs into the Ice Box (a fixed line has been in place on the entry slab). Allow about 15 minutes from the car; expect snow on the approach early in the season.
current.descent: Single-pitch sport route; lower directly from the two-bolt anchor at the top of the pitch back to the base. No walk-off or rappel needed.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted single pitch; a standard sport rack of about 8-10 quickdraws is sufficient to protect the 60 ft (18 m) route, plus a rope long enough to lower a climber that distance.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted; no natural gear needed.

name: East Gully Route (East Peak)
beta: From the trailhead, cross the North Fork Teanaway River and follow talus and snow slopes up to the base of the gully on the east side of the East Peak. The lower gully starts as debris-covered Class 2-3 scrambling, then steepens into Class 4 climbing on poor holds with a trickle of water running down the rock. After roughly 500 ft the gully becomes steep, loose, essentially unprotectable, and wet; most parties exit via a short chimney on climber's right to traverse around this section at low 5th-class difficulty before a horn where a side gully rejoins the main line. Above this the climbing eases somewhat but the rock remains loose ('Cascade ball bearings'), continuing to a final ridge walk to the East Peak summit.
overview: An obscure, unpolished Class 3-4 (low 5th) gully line up the east side of Esmeralda's East Peak — by no means a classic, with the crux low in the gully on wet, friable rock.

current.approach: From the Esmeralda/Ingalls trailhead, cross the North Fork Teanaway River near a jam of small trees, then follow a backcountry route up talus and (early-season) snow slopes to reach the base of the east-facing gully on the East Peak.
current.descent: From the East Peak summit, down-climb/scramble south down talus and scree for roughly 400-500 ft, then traverse gradually south across slopes to intersect the De Roux Creek Trail and follow it down toward the De Roux trailhead. That trailhead is about a mile down the valley from the road-end Esmeralda/Ingalls trailhead where you started, so finish by walking back up the valley along the North Fork Teanaway road or the unmarked path beside it — effectively a loop rather than a reversal of the ascent gully. In mid-June a trail marked on maps below the East Peak could not be found, so expect to descend off-trail to the De Roux path.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack suffices for the modest technical difficulty: a handful of stoppers and cams in the 1 to 1.5 inch range, plus several slings; one recorded ascent used only a single stopper for protection through the crux.
current.pro_needs: Protection is sparse and the rock is friable — treat placements as psychological rather than bombproof, especially through the wet crux section low in the gully.

name: Southwest Slope (De Roux Creek)
beta: From the De Roux trailhead (3,800 ft), follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 roughly 3 miles west up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, passing several waterfalls, to a scree field near the final switchback (~5,600 ft) marked by a house-sized boulder. Leave the trail here and climb straight up a sustained, ~1,100 ft Class 2 scree/talus slope to the west summit (6,776 ft, true high point and register location); many topo maps mark the eastern summit (~10 ft lower) as the true top, so most parties tag both. The upper 100-150 ft is loose broken rock but not technically difficult; no rope is normally needed.
overview: Esmeralda Peaks form a rugged, multi-summit ridge at the south end of the Teanaway Range in the Wenatchee Mountains, straddling the boundary of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 2.5 miles south of Ingalls Peak. The massif has an east and a west summit roughly 10 vertical feet apart, with older topos disagreeing on which is the true high point — most parties tag both. It sits on the USGS Mount Stuart quadrangle and is a popular moderate scramble objective with close-up views of Mt. Stuart and, from the ridge, distant Mt. Rainier. The standard line described here comes from the De Roux Creek valley to the south: a valley trail to a house-sized boulder at its last switchback, then a sustained Class 2 scree and talus slope to the west summit.

current.approach: Start at the De Roux trailhead and campground (~3,800 ft), on the left about 8.5 miles up gravel FR-9737 beyond the end of the paved North Fork Teanaway Road. Take the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 west, crossing the North Fork Teanaway and then De Roux Creek on bridges. About a mile in, keep right where the De Roux spur branches left, on the trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. The trail climbs steadily up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, crosses the creek again on rocks or logs (awkward in snowmelt), passes several waterfalls, and makes its last switchback across a talus ridge at roughly 5,500-5,600 ft, where a house-sized boulder sits beside the tread. Leave the trail there on the boulder's climber's left and head up the hillside on a northeast bearing. Above is about 1,100 ft of sustained Class 2 scree and talus with no marked path; the line beneath the southwest ridge and the talus farther to climber's right both go, and a boulder field farther west is an alternative if the direct slope is too loose. The top 100-150 ft is loose broken rock. The west summit is a walk-up and very slightly higher than the east summit, which is the one the maps mark; most parties tag both. The round trip is about 7 miles with roughly 3,100 ft of gain, and there is no water once you leave the valley trail.
approach_variant_names: Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 to the last switchback
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling. Retrace the ascent line down the Class 2 scree and talus slope, aiming back for the trail's last switchback; staying in the trees beside the boulder field on the way down avoids most of the loose talus. Rejoin the Boulder-De Roux Trail at the house-sized boulder and follow it back down the valley to the De Roux trailhead. The east and west summits are close enough to link along the connecting ridge before descending. No fixed anchors or rope work are reported; the hazards are loose rock underfoot, rockfall onto parties below, and finding the right line back to the switchback in low cloud, since the open slopes look alike.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack needed — this is a non-technical Class 2 scramble with no fixed protection or established rope work.
current.pro_needs: None; a rope/rack is not used on the standard route.
current.rope_note: Class 2 scree/talus scramble from De Roux Creek; no technical gear needed. Ice axe recommended if snow present early season.

name: Eternal Bliss Endured
beta: Begins with low-angle scrambling over a block, then ascends steeper terrain to midpoint anchors; a bulge presents a crux on lichen-covered rock before easier terrain leads to the top.
overview: A two-pitch sport line just right of Crescendo of the Sarcophagus Breathing, longer than it appears due to foreshortening.

current.approach: Just right of Crescendo of the Sarcophagus Breathing, on the climber's right side of a wall marked by distinctive orange lichen.
current.descent: Midpoint anchors let climbers without a 70m rope rethread and lower in two stages rather than needing a single long rappel/lower from the top.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted: 17 bolts to 2 chain anchors.
current.pro_needs: Sport rack of 17 quickdraws.

name: Excavation, AKA The Crack
beta: A mildly overhanging start holds what is likely the pumpiest move of the climb low down, leading into numerous stemming moves up a crack system. A muddy ledge partway up (partially cleaned/"excavated" by early ascentionists, hence the name) breaks the climbing before a thinner, well-protected finishing crack. Currently top-roped off a static line anchored to a tree at the top; bolted anchors are planned but not yet installed.
overview: The obvious crack splitting the left side of the Shuksan Crag main wall — a 50 ft trad/top-rope line climbable as 5.8 rock or, with tools and crampons, as an M5+ dry-tooling test-piece.

current.approach: From Bellingham, drive the Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east through Glacier; continue about 13.3 miles past Glacier to an unpaved turn on the left — Hannegan Pass Road (FS Road 32) — just before the highway crosses the Nooksack River near Milepost 46. Follow Hannegan Pass Road roughly two minutes (a fraction of a mile) to a pullout; the crag is the obvious cliff on the left, only a few feet off the road.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass Road pullout
current.descent: There is no walk-off; climbers lower from the fixed static rope rigged to a tree above the route. Because the existing bolts on the wall are old and rusty, climbers are advised to top-rope rather than lead, using the tree anchor to rig the line from above (scramble/walk around to the top).
current.detailed_rack: Standard trad rack for a short crack: a set of cams from finger to hand size plus a few nuts, with slings for the tree top-anchor; a static rope/cordelette is commonly used to rig the top-rope since there are no bolted anchors yet.
current.pro_needs: Trad gear throughout the crack; no fixed protection on the route itself. Anchor is a tree at the top of the cliff, not bolts.

name: EZ Way
beta: EZ Way is a 5.6 trad climb on Shark Rock's west face. The rock is very solid but protection is extremely difficult due to minute cracks. A classic but serious alpine rock route requiring competent trad climbing skills and protection placement in difficult crack systems.
overview: The first ascent of Shark Rock's west face, a solid volcanic rock route on a seldom-visited formation in the Dark Divide.

current.approach: From Randle, drive south on Forest Road 25 to Forest Road 2551, just south of Elk Pass, then east on FR2551 for about 1.6 miles to an unmarked spur on the left; park at or just past the spur. From the parking spur, short flagged connector paths lead to the Boundary Trail. Follow the Boundary Trail 2.25 miles to Badger Lake, then continue 2.75 miles and about 700 feet of elevation gain to the last switchback below the ridge crest; from there an almost-level traverse through open timber breaks out onto the open west face of Shark Rock.
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the exposed 3rd/4th-class ridge scramble back to the upper belay area near the Alaskan yellow cedar. Rig a rappel from an anchor roughly 10 feet below the cedar and rappel (60m rope recommended) back down to the lower belay bench. From there, downclimb the 3rd/4th-class scramble through the band of small trees and reverse the low-angle traverse across the west face back to the boot path and Boundary Trail.
current.detailed_rack: A single set of small-to-medium wired stoppers plus cams up to a #3 (per the first-ascent party); the lower 30-40 feet is essentially unprotectable, so extra small-to-mid pieces for the crack section above are more useful than a large rack.
current.pro_needs: Protection is minute and marginal for roughly the first 30-40 feet off the belay bench; a standard small-to-medium rack (stoppers and cams to a #3) covers the one crack that does take gear, but climbers should be comfortable with real runouts on otherwise solid rock.
current.rope_note: Short 5.6 trad route at Shark Rock (minor Gifford Pinchot crag); single 60m rope sufficient. One roped pitch, with unroped scrambling below and above it.

name: Face Farce
beta: A few jugs and a fist jam get you through the crux to a bolted anchor shared with Bachelor Party.
overview: Sport climb on Megadike North.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on Megadike North: pull over at 1.1 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, at the spot on the left (SE side) where a dirt road joins the pavement, or drive on to 1.2 miles and use the large pull-off. Cross the main road and pick up the approach trail between the two parking spots, marked by a short steep drainage topped with a downed tree.
current.descent: All Megadike North routes are single-pitch and well within a 60m rope's reach (longest route here is 100 ft); lower straight back to the ground from the chain/shut anchor, no walk-off needed.
current.detailed_rack: 4 bolts to shuts; a standard sport rack of ~10 quickdraws and a 60m rope is plenty for this 35 ft route.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (4 bolts to shuts); no trad gear needed.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Megadike North (The Dikes, WA). 70m recommended given Megadike North's walls up to ~120ft.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Fifth of July Mountain's easiest route is straightforward class 2 hiking/scrambling up its south ridge — no rope or technical gear is needed for the peak itself. One approach starts at the Basalt Pass Trailhead, following the Basalt Ridge crest north past Point 6351 and a saddle below Devils Smoke Stack (a separate, harder class 3 summit), then dropping into a basin and climbing boulder fields and a larch-dotted bench to the peak's south ridge and summit. The longer approach, the one this route plan follows, comes from the Entiat River Trailhead via Myrtle Lake, Larch Lakes, and Cow Creek Pass, climbing the same south ridge from the east. Tread fades to nothing above treeline on both approaches, and route-finding across slick pumice and burned terrain (2020 Chikamin Creek Fire) is part of the challenge.
overview: Fifth of July Mountain (7,696 ft) is a prominent, dry east-Cascades summit in the Entiat Mountains within the Glacier Peak Wilderness, rising above the upper Entiat River valley and the Cow Creek Meadows / Myrtle Lake / Larch Lakes basin in Chelan County. USFS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester named the peak for the day (July 5) he first visited it; its nearest higher neighbor is Chilly Peak (7,960 ft), about 3.8 miles north-northwest. The standard route climbs open south-facing slopes and the south ridge from Cow Creek Meadows, and is popular in early fall as part of a larch-viewing loop through the Larch Lakes basin and Cow Creek Pass.

current.approach: Start at the Entiat River Trailhead (elev. ~3,150 ft) at the end of Entiat River Road (FS Road 51), where a Northwest Forest Pass is required. Follow the Entiat River Trail No. 1400 upstream through mixed forest, gently graded, for about 4 miles. At roughly the 4-mile mark the trail reaches the crossing where a footbridge once stood; the bridge deck burned in the 2015 Wolverine Fire and only the steel I-beams and railing remain, so plan on either crab-walking the exposed beams (some real fall risk, especially with a pack) or fording the Entiat River directly, which can run high and cold with early-season snowmelt — this crossing is the approach's main hazard and should be scouted before committing. Once across, pick up the Cow Creek Meadows Trail No. 1404 and climb steadily northwest through subalpine forest, passing Myrtle Lake (a good water source and camp option) a few tenths of a mile past the river crossing. Continue up-valley into Cow Creek Meadows itself (about 5,000 ft, reached by a steep, sun-exposed climb of roughly 1,300 ft in a mile), an open avalanche-prone basin below the Fifth of July Mountain ridgeline — snow can linger here into July and avalanche debris/downed timber from the slopes above is common, so expect some route-finding through blowdown and brush at the meadow's edges. Above the meadows the trail climbs on to Cow Creek Pass on the mountain's shoulder; leave the trail there and work up open talus and heather slopes on the mountain's south side toward the south ridge, gaining the rest of the height cross-country over scree, boulders and intermittent goat/climber's paths. There is no reliable water above Cow Creek Meadows, so fill up there or at Myrtle Lake. Total one-way distance to the summit is on the order of 8-9 miles with about 4,500 ft of gain, consistent with a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight basecamp at Myrtle Lake, Cow Creek Meadows, or the Larch Lakes.
approach_variant_names: Basalt Ridge crest to Fifth of July Pass
Entiat River and Larch Lakes
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: pick your way back down the open south-facing talus, scree and heather slopes off the south ridge to the trail at Cow Creek Pass, watching footing on the loose rock (more hazardous descending than climbing) and staying alert for parties below if scree is being kicked loose. Follow Cow Creek Meadows Trail No. 1404 back down through the meadows, past Myrtle Lake, and rejoin the Entiat River Trail No. 1400 for the roughly 4-mile walk back down-valley to the trailhead. The Entiat River crossing near the old bridge site (burned I-beams or a ford) is again the key obstacle and is often trickier tired and later in the day when snowmelt flows are higher. This is a walk-off/scramble descent with no technical downclimbing and no rappels required under normal summer conditions; a helmet is worth carrying for the loose south-slope terrain, and an ice axe may be prudent for early-season snow patches on the upper mountain or in Cow Creek Meadows.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for Fifth of July Mountain's standard south-ridge line; it is class 2 talus/boulder scrambling. Parties who detour to bag neighboring Devils Smoke Stack (class 3, with short, exposed steps) may want a short length of rope for confidence, but it is not used on Fifth of July itself.
current.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble on the standard route.
bivy: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
current.rope_note: Inferred as a straightforward Class 2 talus/scree walk-up; no rope or rack needed.

name: Fire on the Mountain
beta: 1,100 ft (333 m) of technical rock across 8 pitches, plus roughly 500 ft of 3rd-class scrambling to the summit. Climbs wild knobs and diorite fins reminiscent of California granite. Pitches are steep, long, and relatively sustained for alpine climbing; rock quality is generally very good but can be lichen-y/dirty in places from low traffic. Generally very good protection, especially at the cruxes, with a couple of runout sections (pitches 2 and 5).
overview: Fire on the Mountain climbs 8 pitches of sustained, well-protected alpine rock (to 5.10d) up Sloan's Southwest Face, joining a major ledge that intersects the Corkscrew Route; from there it's roughly 500 ft of 4th-class/low-5th scrambling to the true summit.

current.approach: From the Mountain Loop Highway, turn onto FR 4096 (Bedal Creek Trailhead spur) and park at the trailhead, 2,790–2,800 ft. Follow the Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old-growth forest along Bedal Creek's steep banks; the maintained tread peters out roughly 1.5–2.5 miles in, at a large brushy washout coming down off the basin below Sloan's West Face. Scramble up the boulder- and blowdown-choked washout — this is the crux of route-finding on the approach — until a cairn marks an exit onto a climber's path (often flagged with pink tape) that switchbacks steeply through forest from about 3,500 ft to 4,900 ft. Above treeline the path crosses talus and a meadow bench (4,900–5,300 ft) with summit views, passes a stagnant tarn near the 5,300 ft saddle between Bedal Peak and Sloan Peak (last reliable water is here or at the cascading streams just below), then continues on rocky, exposed scrambling terrain to about 5,800 ft at the toe of the glacier — crampons/axe may be needed here depending on season. For the Southwest Face (Fire on the Mountain's start), do not follow the standard Corkscrew line onto the glacier; instead cross the low ridge that separates the West Face basin from the Southwest Face basin/meadows to reach the base of the face. Total car-to-base time runs about 3 hours for a fit, familiar party; expect a long day given ~8 pitches of technical climbing still ahead. An alternate approach via the Cougar Creek/North Fork Sauk trailhead (FR 49) converges with the Bedal Creek route around 5,000–5,500 ft but requires fording the North Fork Sauk River, a crossing that is deep, swift, and best avoided solo or in high early-season flow.
approach_variant_names: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
current.descent: From the top of the technical climbing, stash rock gear and follow the upper Corkscrew line roughly 400–500 ft of 3rd/4th class scrambling to the true summit (optional — many parties skip the summit push and head straight for the descent). To descend: return to the gear stash, downclimb a few hundred feet, then drop right down a steep heathered gully to an 'access ramp' — a sound-granite ledge system that is easy 3rd class scrambling over boulders and vegetated steps. Follow the ramp until it necks down to a slabby downclimb. Here parties either continue downclimbing directly to snow (low 5th class, unprotected) or rig one rappel to reach the snowfield below and keep the whole exit at 4th class. Existing rappel tat/anchors have been reported on the ramp system, but they are natural (slung horns/blocks) and of questionable, unverified quality — back them up or build your own rather than trusting them blind. Once on snow, traverse clockwise around the mountain (rope up for any crevassed/glacier travel) back to the Southwest Face basin and reverse the approach. Treat the single rappel as optional/conditions-dependent: in late-season low-snow conditions parties have downclimbed the whole exit with no rope out.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles of cams from roughly #0.2 to #2, a single #3, a full set of stoppers, and lots of alpine draws (doubles of slings recommended).
current.pro_needs: Generally very good protection, especially at the pitch cruxes, but with runout sections on pitch 2 and pitch 5.
bivy: Bivy at the base of Sloan's southwest face
current.rope_note: 8 pitches of 5.10d rock (to a ledge intersecting the Corkscrew Route) plus ~500ft of 4th/low-5th scrambling to the true summit; ~1000ft technical + 500ft scrambling total. Generally good protection at cruxes but runout sections on P2 and P5.

name: Firearms
beta: Begins with an overhanging section, then eases up with a great resting point before the chain anchor.
overview: The first route seen from the trail at Minidike; overhanging start easing to a good rest before the chains.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. For the Minidike, pull off 1.5 miles beyond the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, on the left (SE) side of the road immediately after the bridge over the river. Cross the road, scramble down the bridge abutment, and follow a trail downstream on the NW side.
current.descent: Lower from the chain anchor (7 bolts, shared anchor with the adjacent Cheap Beer route) on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: 7 bolts to chain anchors, shared with Cheap Beer.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted (7 bolts).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at Minidike (The Dikes, WA). Minidike routes are shorter than Megadike; 60m is sufficient.

name: First Amendment
beta: Opens with a 100-foot 5.4 chimney and hand crack, then follows hands-and-fists and finger-crack corners (5.8-5.9) through a choss-cave belay, before a 5.10+ series of corners and roofs taking thin protection (knifeblades/Lost Arrows useful); the 5.11a crux comes right off a belay in super-thin cracks, after which easier pitches join Spontaneity Arete's ridge to the summit. Route lacks a fully sustained or continuously natural line, with some dirty/vegetated cracks in places.
overview: First Amendment (IV 5.11a, 9 pitches) climbs the northwest/west face of Le Petit Cheval at Washington Pass, established by Chris McNamara and Ian Nicholson in September 2009.

current.approach: From the pullout, an unmarked but well-worn climbers' trail drops steeply from the west/southwest end of the turnout through loose dirt and rock into the trees, marked intermittently by cairns. The path crosses Early Winters Creek (on logs) before climbing into an open rocky drainage/talus below the formation; the final approach to the base involves loose 3rd/4th-class slabs, with sandy access ledges and a fixed rope on parts of the standard line.
approach_variant_names: Highway turnout east of Washington Pass, then a long ledge traverse across the face
current.descent: The route joins Spontaneity Arête for its final pitches, so descend that route's line: rappel it, or take the third-class gully on climbers' right, which is faster but loose.
current.detailed_rack: Cams from finger-size to about 3 inches, with doubles/triples in thin/finger sizes for the sustained thin cracks of the upper pitches (roughly pitches 6-8); small wires and TCUs; some parties have suggested knifeblades and Lost Arrow pitons would help protect the thin, sparse crux pitches.
rack: Small nut set + spare purple TCU/small cam
Single 60m rope, which also serves the rappel descent
current.pro_needs: Protection on the upper pitches (especially the 5.11a crux) is thin and sparse — this is not a well-protected sport-style outing.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: One 60m rope. The descent rappels down the neighbouring arete are spaced for a single 60m rope, and a few of them use its full length.

name: Fish & Whistle
beta: Established by Darin Berdinka on September 11, 2017. Climbs a friction slab past 5 bolts, an easier bolted slab with a fixed pin, a long protectable seam pitch mixing gear and bolts, a short bolted connector pitch, and a final progressively harder face pitch to the top. Rock quality on this part of the face is generally excellent; pitches 1/2 and 3/4 can be readily linked with a 60m rope.
overview: Fish & Whistle climbs the broad center slab of Vesper Peak's north face, just left of True Grit. Established by local climber Darin Berdinka on September 11, 2017, it is the hardest and most sustained of Vesper's moderate face routes — five pitches of mostly bolt-protected friction and seam climbing on excellent, largely clean granite.

current.approach: Same approach as True Grit and Ragged Edge: Sunrise Mine Trail #707 from the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, through Wirtz Basin and Headlee Pass (~4,720 ft, 2.7 mi, loose rock/rockfall in the narrow couloir), down to Vesper Creek and up a short rise to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, ~4,950 ft, ~3.5 mi/~2,700 ft gain — last water), then off-trail up the talus ridge to the Vesper-Wolf col and across the exposed heather ledge system at ~5,800 ft (slick when wet, holds snow into mid-to-late summer — ice axe useful early season). Fish & Whistle's start is not a separate landmark on this traverse — it's a large tree roughly 50 ft left (west) of the True Grit start, on the talus/boulder apron directly below the north face, so simply continue the same ledge traverse slightly past True Grit's start to find it. Plan 3+ hours from the trailhead to the base of the route.
approach_variant_names: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
current.descent: Fish & Whistle climbs the same upper north-face headwall as True Grit and finishes in the same general area near the top of the face/summit ridge, so the standard exit is almost certainly the same walk-off used for True Grit and Ragged Edge: scramble down the southeast side (a seasonal snow slope early on, open slabs/talus by late summer) back to the Vesper-Wolf saddle, then down to Vesper Lake and out the Sunrise Mine Trail. No rappel anchors or rap-specific beta for this route were found in any published or trip-report account. Given its harder, more sustained bolt-protected pitches, a party unable to finish the walk-off (e.g., benighted or in bad weather) could retreat by rappelling the bolted anchors pitch-by-pitch with a single 60m rope, but this is not the documented standard descent.
current.detailed_rack: Mostly bolt-protected with gear-augmented seam/crack sections: 10 draws, a set of small-to-medium stoppers, and a single cam set from tiny to 0.75 Camalot (extra finger sizes helpful on P3).
current.pro_needs: Predominantly bolted; gear is mainly a backup on the P3 seam pitch. A 60m rope lets parties link P1/P2 and P3/P4.
bivy: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass

name: Flight of the Falcon
beta: One of the best remote alpine rock routes in the North Cascades (listed among the 15 best routes in the Cascades). Mostly sustained ~5.9 climbing with brief 5.10 cruxes on Pitches 3 and 6; 34 protection bolts total and bolted belay anchors up to Pitch 7. Pitch 6 is the main crux, face climbing up a green-tinted slab; Pitch 7 tops out at 'Falcon's Perch,' an exposed viewpoint. Pairs well with Roan Wall - Center Stage for a big alpine linkup day for fast parties.
overview: A 9-pitch, 800-foot Grade III-ish line up the steep south face of Salish Peak, a striking spire just northeast of Three Fingers, climbing ramps, corners and short steep crux sections at a sustained 5.9-ish grade with two harder 5.10 pitches.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. The route is still far above: climb the bolted 5.8 slab and the dirty low-fifth crack to the foot of Roan Wall, scramble up its left side to the saddle where Salish Peak comes into view, and cross the high basin to the toe of the south face, about 6 hours from the car in all. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
current.descent: Two descent options exist. Most parties rappel from the anchor atop Pitch 7 ('Falcon's Perch') using double 60m ropes back down the route. Parties who continue to the summit can instead walk off to the left (west), a descent that takes about 40 minutes from the summit back down to packs at the base, navigating brushy, low-angle terrain.
current.detailed_rack: Wires, a single set of cams tips to #3, and about 12 quickdraws/slings; bring 2x60m ropes if rappelling.
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolt-protected with some natural gear placements on lower pitches; a single rack to #3 plus wires covers the route.
bivy: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
